912aa786b62b1315: LAGOS: A Nigerian Air Force plane crashed on Monday in the country's southwest, killing all 32 people on board, President Bola Tinubu said, declaring three days of national mourning.
It is one the worst air disasters in recent years in Africa's most populous country.

The passenger aircraft was on a "routine mission" from Benin City in southern Nigeria to the economic hub of Lagos when it went down at Igbokoda in southwestern Ondo state shortly after 9am, the president and the air force said.
"The president extends his deepest condolences to the family of the 25 passengers and seven crew members involved," Tinubu's office said in a statement.
"This is a painful moment for our armed forces and for the entire nation," he said.
Tinubu's spokesman Bayo Onanuga said in a later statement that the president "has declared a three-day national mourning for Air Force personnel who died in the crash".
He also directed that flags be flown at half-staff across the country to pay respect to the officers.
"The Air Force will release the identities of the victims after notifying their families," the presidency said.
The plane crashed near a naval base, according to the presidency and the aviation minister Festus Keyamo.
Both described it as an ATR-42 - a twin-engine turboprop that the manufacturers say can carry between 30 and 50 passengers
A video circulating on social media showed a small crowd gathered near a river while rescuers searched the area by boat.
The president said he had "directed the Nigerian Air Force to immediately commence a thorough investigation into the cause of the crash to prevent future occurrences".
Noise like thunder

Dayo Akinte, 39, a firewood hawker who lives about a kilometre from where the accident occurred, described to AFP hearing a sound she thought was "thunder" at the time she believed the plane went down.
Since the crash, "three aircraft have also been flying over the scene", she said by phone.
She said someone who went fishing in the swamp alerted the nearby naval base and people in the town about the crash.
Airforce spokesman Ehimen Ejodame earlier said "search and rescue operations" were ongoing "in coordination with relevant authorities and emergency response agencies".
Police also confirmed the accident but provided no details.
Igbokoda is located in Ilaje, an oil-producing region in southern Nigeria.

In May 2021, Nigeria's top-ranking army commander, Lieutenant General Ibrahim Attahiru, and 10 other officers were killed when their plane crashed in bad weather while trying to land at northern Kaduna state airport.
Seven people died when a military plane crashed into a house in northern Nigeria, killing everyone on board in Aug 2015.
Earlier that same month, a helicopter crashed into a lagoon in Lagos, killing six, including the American pilot.
20503b8734129246: LONDON: British author Jeffrey Archer, who penned a series of best-selling novels, served as a Conservative MP and was convicted of perjury, died suddenly at 86, his publisher HarperCollins said.
Archer died "suddenly and peacefully at his home between writing sessions" on Monday, HarperCollins said.
His editor, Kate Elton, called him a "master storyteller and an editor's dream."
The writer had been due to appear at Cheltenham Literary Festival this week to discuss "Adam and Eve", what he described as his final novel after 50 years of storytelling.
It was due to be published Tuesday.
The Sun tabloid reported that he had been signing books for fans at an event in London on Sunday.
Archer had revealed in 2014 that he had been diagnosed with prostate cancer.
The author led a life as colourful as the characters in his novels, which sold over 300 million copies, according to his website.
Talented and ambitious, he was a high flyer who could never quite escape the whiff of scandal despite a talent for bouncing back from humiliating setbacks.
Politics and sex were the ingredients which ensured his success as a novelist.
But in real life the combination led to the downfall of the man who once hoped to become mayor of London.
He was tried for perjury and perverting the course of justice after a friend admitted he had supplied a false alibi during a libel case the peer brought against the Daily Star tabloid in 1987.
Archer had sued the newspaper over a claim he had slept with a prostitute, winning £500,000 in damages.
Ambitious from his earliest years, Archer used his charm and fund-raising abilities to climb almost to the top of the Conservative Party.
MP AT 29
He joined the Tories while a student at Britain's prestigious Oxford University and in 1969 won a resounding by-election victory to become a member of parliament at the age of 29.
His parliamentary career came to an abrupt end in 1974 when he was brought to the brink of bankruptcy by the collapse of a Canadian industrial cleaning company in which he had invested.

However, with typical resilience he used his experiences as material for his first book "Not A Penny More, Not A Penny Less", published in 1975, the first of a series of blockbusters set in the worlds of high finance and politics.
Panned by the critics, they nevertheless earned him a fortune and Archer nursed hopes of a political revival while using his contacts and persuasiveness to raise millions of pounds for the Tories.
In 1985, his labours were recognised by then prime minister Margaret Thatcher, who named him Conservative deputy chairman, describing him as a model Tory high achiever.
SCANDALS
But a year after his appointment, he was forced to resign by what he described as a "lack of judgment" after sending £2,000 to a prostitute, Monica Coghlan.
He maintained he only paid the money to help her escape hounding from reporters by going abroad and sued the Daily Star for suggesting otherwise.
In 1992 he was recommended by Thatcher's successor John Major for a peerage, entitling him to sit in the House of Lords, the upper chamber of parliament.
In 1999, he launched a campaign to become the Tory party's candidate to become the first elected mayor of London.

But months later the claim emerged that he had asked a friend, Ted Francis to provide him with a false alibi against the Daily Star. This forced him to abandon his bid and he was expelled from the party.
In 2001 he went on trial and was found guilty of perjury and perverting the course of justice. He was sentenced to four years in prison, but was granted parole in 2003.
Archer's long-suffering wife Mary, a scientist, stood behind her husband in his many mishaps.
Famously praised for her "fragrance" by the judge in the 1987 libel trial, she once said: "We've explored the further reaches of 'for better and for worse' than most couples."
Archer retired from the House of Lords in 2024. His wife is Chancellor of the University of Buckingham.

f8402d540613b55b: PETALING JAYA: The differing tones of Umno president Ahmad Zahid Hamidi and his deputy, Mohamad Hasan, on the party’s renewed ties with PAS reflect the different political calculations they face, says an analyst.

Syaza Shukri of International Islamic University Malaysia said that while Zahid and Mohamad were both looking at what they believed was best for Umno, their positions in the party shaped how they approached possible cooperation with PAS.
She said Zahid appeared more pragmatic because he also had to consider what kind of arrangement would allow him to retain his position.

Mohamad, who is known as Tok Mat, "is not thinking so much about that because he’s not at the top," she said. "That’s why his consideration is more on what is best for Umno because win or lose, pact or no pact, he remains number two,” she told FMT.

Syaza said Zahid remained the key decision-maker on major party matters. “Zahid is still very powerful. He gives the impression that he allows dissent, but when it comes to what matters, it will be Zahid’s decision,” she said.

Her comments come after former Umno Supreme Council member Puad Zarkashi had observed that Zahid played up talk of the “blue wave” after Barisan Nasional and Perikatan Nasional’s victory in Negeri Sembilan.

Puad said Mohamad appeared to be more cautious, having urged PAS to prove its sincerity through a snap election in PAS-led Terengganu, a call later rejected by PAS deputy president Tuan Ibrahim Tuan Man, who said the Terengganu state election and the next general election were separate matters.
Awang Azman Pawi of Universiti Malaya said the situation should not be viewed as a split in Umno, but as different strategic positions within the party.

He said Zahid appeared to be keeping political options open, while Mohamad was stressing that any cooperation must be based on reciprocity and mutual respect. “They have different tones, which are not necessarily contradictory. One creates room for engagement, while the other defines the conditions for it,” he said.
Syaza said that if Umno decided to work with PAS, it would still need to ensure PAS did not gain excessive leverage in negotiations.

She said that while the initial commitment to cooperate on the basis of avoiding a split in Malay votes is easier for the grassroots to accept, the principle of give-and-take becomes difficult in terms of seat allocations, as the parties’ machinery might resist giving up incumbent seats despite the decisions made by top leaders.
c15aac3e08dfd642: PETALING JAYA: Nada berbeza antara Presiden Umno Zahid Hamidi dan timbalannya Mohamad Hasan mengenai hubungan yang kembali terjalin dengan PAS, mencerminkan pertimbangan politik berbeza oleh kedua-dua pemimpin itu, kata seorang penganalisis.

Syaza Shukri dari Universiti Islam Antarabangsa Malaysia berkata, walaupun Zahid dan Mohamad sama-sama melihat apa yang dianggap terbaik untuk Umno, kedudukan mereka dalam parti membentuk cara masing-masing mendekati kemungkinan kerjasama dengan PAS.
Katanya, Zahid kelihatan lebih pragmatik kerana beliau juga perlu mempertimbangkan bentuk kerjasama yang membolehkannya mengekalkan kedudukannya.

Mohamad, yang dikenali sebagai Tok Mat, "tidak begitu memikirkan perkara itu kerana beliau bukan di kedudukan teratas,” katanya. “Sebab itu pertimbangannya lebih tertumpu kepada apa yang terbaik untuk Umno kerana menang atau kalah, kerjasama atau tidak, beliau kekal sebagai orang nombor dua,” katanya kepada FMT.

Syaza berkata Zahid kekal sebagai pembuat keputusan utama dalam perkara besar parti. “Zahid masih sangat berkuasa. Beliau memberi gambaran bahawa beliau membenarkan perbezaan pendapat, tetapi apabila menyentuh perkara penting, keputusan tetap di tangan Zahid,” katanya.

Kenyataan beliau dibuat selepas bekas anggota Majlis Kerja Tertinggi (MKT) Umno Puad Zarkashi menyatakan bahawa Zahid memperhebatkan naratif 'gelombang biru' selepas Barisan Nasional (BN) dan Perikatan Nasional (PN) menang di Negeri Sembilan.

Puad berkata Mohamad kelihatan lebih berhati-hati apabila menggesa PAS membuktikan keikhlasannya menerusi pilihan raya mengejut di Terengganu yang ditadbir PAS. Gesaan itu kemudian ditolak Timbalan Presiden PAS Tuan Ibrahim Tuan Man yang berkata PRN Terengganu dan pilihan raya umum akan datang merupakan dua perkara berasingan.
Awang Azman Awang Pawi dari Universiti Malaya berkata keadaan itu tidak seharusnya dilihat sebagai perpecahan dalam Umno, sebaliknya sebagai perbezaan pendirian strategik dalam parti.
Katanya, Zahid dilihat mahu mengekalkan pelbagai pilihan politik terbuka, manakala Mohamad menegaskan bahawa sebarang kerjasama mesti berasaskan prinsip timbal balik dan saling menghormati.
“Nada mereka berbeza, tetapi tidak semestinya bercanggah. Satu pihak membuka ruang untuk rundingan, manakala satu lagi menetapkan syarat untuk rundingan itu,” katanya.
Syaza berkata sekiranya Umno memutuskan untuk bekerjasama dengan PAS, parti itu masih perlu memastikan PAS tidak memperoleh pengaruh berlebihan dalam rundingan.

Katanya, komitmen awal untuk bekerjasama atas dasar mengelakkan perpecahan undi Melayu lebih mudah diterima akar umbi, namun prinsip saling memberi dan menerima menjadi sukar apabila melibatkan pembahagian kerusi, kerana jentera parti mungkin menolak untuk melepaskan kerusi penyandang walaupun keputusan telah dibuat oleh pemimpin tertinggi.
698617ce93cbb33d: SHAH ALAM: Nur Ahmad Faiz Azmi spent about a month teaching himself how to build a delivery app. Getting someone to actually use it took considerably longer.

The idea for Misi Delivery took shape during the pandemic, when the former clothing-printing entrepreneur began paying closer attention to the complaints he was hearing from food delivery riders and merchants.
Riders spoke about low pay and the risks of the job, while food sellers were concerned about commissions eating into their earnings.

“During Covid-19, I observed that the only form of business that could survive was delivery. At the same time, I heard many complaints from riders about low pay, which was sometimes not commensurate with the work involved, on top of the various safety risks they faced,” he told Bernama.
“Then I learnt that merchants also had to pay high commission rates to service providers, which reduced their profits. All this motivated me to develop my app.”
The problem? Faiz had never built an app before.

An SPM holder who had previously spent two years running a clothing-printing business, he turned to the internet to teach himself what he needed to know. YouTube became part of the learning process, along with a platform that allows users to build applications without conventional coding.
The learning curve was not cheap. Faiz invested about RM30,000 of his own money, generated from his printing business. Mistakes during development pushed the cost higher.
“But that is part of the learning process. I kept trying different approaches and eventually succeeded."

While building the app took about a month, convincing people to use it took eight. Faiz had assumed the social media following he had built through his clothing business would translate easily into users for his new venture - but the response was far slower than expected.
When the first order finally came through in Puncak Alam, Faiz delivered it himself. Beyond the sale, the moment gave him something more important: small proof that the system could work.
Slowly but surely, orders gradually increased and the service expanded beyond Puncak Alam into areas including Meru, Pulau Indah and Klang.
Nearly five years on, Faiz says the platform has around 200,000 registered vendors and some 40,000 riders across several states, including the Klang Valley, Perlis, Perak and Labuan.

His business model differs from some larger delivery platforms in one key respect: merchants are not charged a commission on each order, while riders are paid according to distance travelled. Customers instead pay a service fee when placing an order through the app.

“Through Misi, merchants can maintain the same prices as those offered at their premises and retain the full amount from their sales, while food delivery riders receive a minimum payment of RM5 for 5km, with the rate increasing according to the distance travelled,” he explained.
For Faiz, some of the most satisfying signs of growth are less about overall sales figures than seeing individual vendors build a steady stream of orders.

During a visit to Labuan, he met a nasi katok seller who told him the stall was receiving more than 3,000 orders a month through the app. “I was surprised,” Faiz said. “That is an extraordinary achievement.”

The transition from printing T-shirts to running a digital delivery platform also meant entering an industry he barely knew. That unfamiliarity attracted scepticism, particularly when he was trying to establish a new platform alongside much larger names in the sector.
But rather than abandon the idea, Faiz kept adjusting the service and expanding its reach as users slowly came on board.

Today, a team of 14 helps manage the operation. The platform has also begun extending beyond food delivery into other areas, including services offered by tradespeople such as electricians, plumbers and air-conditioning installers.
For Faiz, the most formative part of the journey may still be those first eight quiet months, when the app existed but almost nobody seemed interested.
This taught him that learning how to build something was only the beginning; the harder part was earning enough trust for somebody to click “order” for the first time.
e332f57825407211: THE HAGUE: The International Criminal Court on Monday unsealed arrest warrants for two Afghan education ministers accused of committing crimes against humanity through the Taliban government's restrictions on women and girls.
The warrants, for Habibullah Agha, minister of education, and Neda Mohammad Nadeem, minister of higher education, were issued on September 9, 2025 and remained under seal until Monday.

The two officials are accused of gender-based persecution linked to policies that have barred girls aged over 12 from school and excluded women from higher education following the Taliban's return to power in August 2021.
The ICC warrants were likely to increase international pressure on the Taliban government.
AFP has approached Taliban authorities for comment.

The two warrants against the ministers were issued after the ICC, in July 2025, authorised warrants for Afghanistan's Supreme Taliban Leader Haibatullah Akhundzada and Supreme Court President Abdul Hakim Haqqani, parts of which have been made public.
Both Agha and Nadeem have played key roles in implementing the supreme leader's vision for Afghanistan.
"There are reasonable grounds to believe" the suspects committed "the crime against humanity of persecution on gender grounds", the court said.

It said the persecution was directed against women and girls, and the deprivation of their fundamental rights was committed "in connection with" other alleged crimes under the Taliban government's policies, including "imprisonment, torture, rape and enforced disappearance."
The court said the alleged crimes were committed in Afghanistan from the Taliban's takeover until at least January 20, 2025.
'WORSENING' OPPRESSION

The ICC's disclosure of the warrants came the same day the UN Human Rights Council urged the Taliban authorities to repeal their "worsening" and "systematic oppression of all women and girls in Afghanistan."
The council's 47 member countries unanimously criticised that discrimination "and the harms that it has entrenched, which are unbearable, unjustifiable and should shock the conscience of humanity."

The ICC's Pre-Trial Chamber II said it decided to unseal all four warrants, with redactions, after concluding that doing so would not unduly affect ongoing investigations and could "prevent the commission of further crimes by the suspects."
Publication could also "promote cooperation by the international community... in relation to the situation in Afghanistan", it said.
Afghans across the country have told AFP journalists of severe mental health problems tied to the education ban, with teenage girls and women mostly staying at home.
Afghan universities are now men-only zones, where smartphones are banned and students can be chastised if their beards are not long enough.
Some women and girls have tried to continue their education by studying online, but their efforts are hampered by internet and electricity problems across Afghanistan.
Women are increasingly absent from public life and need to abide by a strict dress code when they leave home, covering everything but their eyes.
They are banned from most jobs and a host of public places, including parks, and must have a close male relative escort them on long journeys.
The higher education ban has led to staff shortages in hospitals, multiple healthcare workers have told AFP, as women are no longer allowed to qualify as doctors.

d2135b305279b13f: MICHIGAN: Former president Barack Obama and president Donald Trump both plan to campaign in Michigan during the coming weeks in a showdown to bolster their candidates, especially in the key Senate race between Democrat Abdul El-Sayed and opponent Mike Rogers, just ahead of the Nov 3 election.

Obama’s Oct 24 appearance - coming about a month after former vice president Kamala Harris campaigned with El-Sayed - underscores the stakes for Democrats in Michigan, long seen as a must-win for the party if it wants to retake the Senate.
In addition to El-Sayed, the rally will feature Michigan secretary of state Jocelyn Benson, who is running for governor, according to a statement Monday from the state’s Democratic Party.
Several polls show El-Sayed within the margin of error in his race against former Republican representative Mike Rogers, with the campaign becoming one of the most expensive in this midterm cycle.
More than US$280 million has been spent on advertising so far, according to AdImpact.

Democrats need to flip four seats to take a majority in the Senate and while more races nationally have become competitive, holding Michigan following the retirement of Democratic Senator Gary Peters is seen as essential to that effort.

Trump said at the White House on Monday that he will be in Michigan “in about a week and a half.” He was last in the state in July when he held a rally at the General Motors vehicle testing ground in Milford outside Detroit. The president has spent his time campaigning recently in the Republican-led states of Alabama and Oklahoma.

The question for Republicans is whether Trump will help Rogers. The Epic MRA poll said 57% of Michigan voters polled see Trump unfavourably. Governor Gretchen Whitmer fares next worst with a 42% unfavourable rating.

El-Sayed has been working to court Michigan’s Black voters, who largely backed his Democratic opponent during the primary. A recent poll conducted in the state by Epic MRA in late August had El-Sayed leading Rogers among all voters by 47% to 43%. The same poll had 77% of Black voters backing the Democrat.

Obama has kept a relatively low profile in midterm races so far, though he did travel to Texas to support Senate candidate James Talarico and Gina Hinojosa, the Democratic candidate for governor, at a taco restaurant in Austin in May.

3d1e1e4ff652a987: LOS ANGELES: Former Spurs, Chelsea and Paris Saint-Germain coach Mauricio Pochettino said he tried to sign striker Jonathan David multiple times with his previous clubs, as he prepares his US side to face Canada Tuesday.
David has started the season in blistering form with Atletico Madrid, which he joined on loan last month after a difficult spell at Juventus.

He has scored three goals in as many games for Atletico, and is expected to lead the line for Canada when the North American rivals clash in an international friendly at Allianz Field in Minnesota on Tuesday.
"When we were in different clubs, he always was on our radar to try to sign him. That is true," said Pochettino.

"Not only here or in Europe, but in the world," he added.

Nicknamed the "Iceman," he joined Serie A giants Juventus on a free transfer in 2025, where his impact was more limited and he scored just eight goals.

"Now seeing him in La Liga in a club like Atletico Madrid with a coach like Diego Simeone is fantastic," said Pochettino, who played and coached in Spain's La Liga with Espanyol.

The US clash with Canada is the fourth of an intense international window for Pochettino's team.

The US beat Peru 4-1, Chile 4-2 and Mexico 3-0, with teenagers Cavan Sullivan, Julian Hall and Mathis Albert all among the goalscorers.
Canada also racked up wins over Chile and Peru, with David bagging the sole goal in the victory over Chile.
Los Angeles FC striker Jacob Shaffelburg was on target twice in Canada's 2-0 defeat of Peru on Saturday.
Pochettino said he expected Jesse Marsch's men and their supporters to be fired up for the clash with Canada's giant neighbor to the south.
"It's obvious that every time that we play against teams like Canada or Mexico, always the competitivity is there, and the fans want to win," he said.
"I think we all know what it means to play against Mexico and Canada," he added.
bc84107251a985f1: BEIJING: Novak Djokovic advanced to the China Open final on Monday after Daniil Medvedev was disqualified late in the second set, when a ball that came off the Russian's racquet hit a spectator.
A man sitting in the stands behind Medvedev's side of the court was seen holding his face and escorted from his seat after being hit, as Djokovic was serving for the match with the score at 7-5, 5-3.

"Terribly sorry to the spectator, first of all," he told reporters afterwards, adding it was "100 percent an accident" and that he wished to apologise to the fan in person.
"The ball was bouncing back, so I tried to, like, just hit it anywhere, so it doesn't go out from the court," he said.

Djokovic was red-faced and hunched over between points, with both players forcing each other through gruelling rallies, until the Serbian took control in the second set.
The 39-year-old put on a dazzling performance and saved 16 break points across the match, diving at the baseline and sprinting to the net.
"I didn't see what happened, to be honest," Djokovic told the crowd after the fan was hit.
"I'm sure that Daniil didn't... do it intentionally. It happened by accident. Sorry for the crowd," he said, adding that it had been a tough contest.
"I know the feeling," Djokovic told reporters later, recounting his own disqualification from the 2020 US Open after accidentally hitting a ball at a line judge.
"It's horrible... but it happens," he said.

"I was just angry, wanted to change something, because clearly it wasn't working," the 25-year-old from Poland said on court.
"Sometimes if you care a bit less because you're... probably going to lose, it also helps you a bit," she told reporters.
She will face American teenager Iva Jovic for a spot in the quarter-finals.
China's Zheng Qinwen was tested by Marie Bouzkova, enduring her third three-setter of the tournament to beat the Czech player 7-6 (7/3), 4-6, 7-5.
She pulled out some of her most accurate tennis to clinch the last two games and win when 27th-ranked Bouzkova fired long.
"I gave everything," said Zheng, who had already spent more than five hours on court in the first two rounds.
"Truthfully speaking, I felt a lot of pressure today," the 23-year-old told her home crowd, thanking fans for their support.
Zheng, the current world number 54, next plays 118th-ranked Alina Charaeva, who sent out top seed Elena Rybakina in the second round.
Wimbledon champion Linda Noskova also advanced and will face Ekaterina Alexandrova in the last 16, while Ukraine's Elina Svitolina will play American Ann Li.

7646046f64fbac3b: PETALING JAYA: Developers of AI chatbots and apps targeting children will be required to incorporate safety features under the proposed Artificial Intelligence (AI) Governance Bill, says digital minister Gobind Singh Deo.

In a written parliamentary reply, Gobind said child protection was being "comprehensively" integrated into the bill, which was being drafted as a foundational framework that could adapt to emerging technology risks.
He said the bill would take a risk-based approach, requiring developers of apps or chatbots aimed at children to incorporate "safety-by-design" measures.
"This includes requiring regular risk impact assessments and filtering harmful content to prevent the psychological manipulation of children," he said.
Gobind said bot disclosure – notifying users that they are interacting with an AI system rather than with a human – would be enforced through a "targeted mechanism" rather than a blanket requirement.

He said the need for disclosure would be determined based on an application’s risk level, sector-specific requirements, and specific laws or sectoral codes of ethics to be issued by the regulator proposed under the bill and by the minister.

Under this phased approach, AI service providers would eventually have to display clear notices informing users that they are interacting with AI, particularly for applications classified as high-risk, he said.

Gobind said the bill’s legal controls would be reinforced through the National Guidelines on AI Governance and Ethics, enforcement of the Online Safety Act, and digital literacy initiatives such as "CyberSAFE untuk Rakyat", a free cybersecurity awareness programme.

He was responding to a question from Riduan Rubin (independent-Tenom) on the safeguards in the AI Governance Bill to mitigate the risks of children using AI chatbots and whether the government would make bot disclosure mandatory to protect minors’ cognitive awareness.
Yesterday, Gobind said the government expected to table the AI Governance Bill in the Dewan Rakyat early next year instead of this year.
He said the government was still drafting the bill, and the level of control and obligations imposed would be assessed based on the potential harm posed by an AI system.

8ec129d5f353814e: UNITED NATIONS: United Nations secretary general Antonio Guterres on Monday called for a permanent ceasefire in Gaza ahead of the third anniversary of the Oct 7, 2023 Hamas attack on Israel.

"It is time for the ceasefire to become permanent. It is time to allow humanitarian assistance at scale. And it is time to respect international law," Guterres said in a statement, calling for a "political path to lasting peace across the whole region."

"Let this anniversary mark not only another year of mourning, but also a renewed determination to build a different future: one in which Israelis and Palestinians can live side by side in peace and security, with their rights, dignity, and aspirations fulfilled," Guterres said.

The UN chief acknowledged Israel's casualties in the statement, calling the Hamas attack "abhorrent" for "killing more than 1,200 Israelis and foreign nationals" and the hostage-taking of another 251 people.
Guterres also said Palestinians in Gaza have faced a "massive loss of life, displacement and destruction," without specifying their death toll.
"Their suffering, too, demands an end, now," Guterres said.

Israel's years-long military campaign in Gaza has killed more than 74,200 people according to the Palestinian Health Ministry, which is under Hamas' authority and whose figures are deemed reliable by the UN.

Guterres acknowledged that a brief ceasefire, announced by US President Donald Trump in October 2025, "brought some relief. But it has yet to deliver security, adequate humanitarian assistance or a credible path to recovery and peace."
Israel, which still controls most of Gaza, refuses to withdraw its soldiers until Hamas' disarmament has been verified.
Hamas, for its part, has advocated for gradual disarmament rather than immediate and unilateral surrender of its arsenal.

Since the 2023 attacks, Israel has waged military attacks on several fronts, notably invading southern Lebanon to confront Hezbollah, the Islamist movement backed by Tehran, and launching war against Iran in late February alongside the United States.

f7822292d13bbc34: KUALA LUMPUR: The failure to remit RM314 million in government revenue collected by My E.G. Sdn Bhd and Zetrix AI Bhd between May 19 and Sept 30 has raised broader concerns about governance, financial controls and accountability, the Public Accounts Committee (PAC) said.

Its chairman, Datuk Mas Ermieyati Samsudin, said the matter went beyond the issue of payment arrears, particularly as the two companies, which are under the My E.G. Group, were entrusted with collecting revenue on behalf of the government.
She said there were many questions that needed to be answered.

"Among them are how such a large amount of RM314 million could have accumulated without being remitted during that period and what monitoring and control mechanisms were established by the government?
"Also, were the terms of the agreement or concession fully complied with and, most importantly, were the interests of the government and public funds sufficiently protected?" she said when contacted.

She said the government must not only explain how the money would be recovered, but also how the situation could have occurred to the point that 35 reminder notices had to be issued and what action would be taken to ensure such a matter did not recur.

Asked whether the PAC might open proceedings into the matter, Mas Ermieyati said the committee had decided that its priority was to complete ongoing proceedings and reports, which were at various stages.
"At this stage, it is most likely that the PAC will not add a new subject to its proceedings. But this does not mean the RM314 million issue should escape public scrutiny and accountability."
Malaysia Corruption Watch (MCW) president Jais Abdul Karim said the short period from May to September did not make the governance issue any less serious.

"In fact, RM314 million accumulating within just over four months raises an important question about the effectiveness of the collection, reconciliation and remittance controls governing third-party collection agents."
He said MCW was concerned by the disclosure that 35 reminder notices had been issued and four engagement sessions held, yet the arrears continued to grow.
"Even more serious is the disclosure that a RM231 million cheque submitted by the company was not processed by the bank on the company's instructions.
"Government revenue collected by an appointed agent is not the company's money. It must be remitted promptly and fully to the government in accordance with the agreed terms."
He said MCW supported the suspension of My E.G. and Zetrix AI as collection agents and the government's efforts to recover the full RM314 million immediately.
"There should be a transparent review to establish how such a substantial amount was allowed to accumulate despite repeated notices and engagements."
He said the government should review whether safeguards, including settlement timelines, bank arrangements, guarantees, monitoring mechanisms and enforcement triggers, were sufficiently robust.
905d43b1543b598c: KUALA LUMPUR, Oct 6 — A bottle of cooking oil, a set of car tyres and a pair of rubber gloves may appear to have little in common.
Yet each begins, in one way or another, with commodities produced by the country’s plantation sector.
Those commodities do not stop at the plantation, as they are processed into products used by consumers and businesses, while also contributing to the country’s exports.
So what does the plantation and commodities sector actually cover, and why has the government proposed RM425.65 million for the Ministry of Plantation and Commodities under Budget 2027?
How will Malaysians “feel” the impact of this allocation?
Let’s take a look at what the ministry covers, where its commodities end up and how they make their way from plantations and smallholdings to consumers and export markets.
The plantation and commodities sector
The ministry oversees commodities including palm oil, rubber, cocoa, pepper, timber, kenaf, sago and tobacco, as well as related downstream activities.
These commodities move through a wider supply chain, from plantations and smallholdings to processing and manufacturing before reaching consumers or overseas markets.
Smallholders, or pekebun kecil, are individual farmers or families who cultivate relatively small areas of land rather than operating large commercial plantations.
They are an important part of the commodity supply chain, particularly in oil palm and rubber.

Plantation and Commodities Minister Datuk Seri Noraini Ahmad has said empowering smallholders through quality inputs, good agricultural practices and support for replanting programmes is one of the ministry’s priorities to improve productivity and income.
Where does it show up in everyday life?
Cooking oil and food
Palm oil is perhaps the most familiar example.
Harvested oil palm fruit is used to make cooking oil and can also be found in a range of everyday products, including margarine, biscuits, bread, chocolate, instant noodles and other processed foods.
In the bathroom, palm-derived ingredients are also used in products such as soap, shampoo and cosmetics.
In 2024, oil palm contributed RM38.1 billion, or 36.8 per cent, of Malaysia’s agricultural value added, making it the largest contributor within the agriculture sector.
Oil palm also extends to markets abroad.
According to the Malaysian Palm Oil Board, palm oil and palm-based products generated RM112.64 billion in exports in 2025.
Tyres, gloves and rubber products
Rubber is another direct link between plantations, industry and consumers’ everyday lives.
Natural rubber and rubber-based materials are used in products such as medical gloves, tyres, rubber hoses, seals, belts and footwear.
There is also a connection between smallholders and manufacturers producing these products, as well as the healthcare, automotive and manufacturing sectors that use them.
These products are also exported, making rubber important not only as a farm commodity but also as an industrial raw material.
Apart from palm oil and rubber, cocoa, pepper, timber, kenaf and sago are other familiar commodities that appear in households or businesses.
What does the RM425m cover?
The proposed amount under Budget 2027 covers four initiatives under the Ministry of Plantation and Commodities.
Its focus is on oil palm smallholder replanting, farm roads, disaster and disease control and support for downstream agro-commodity entrepreneurs.
The largest allocation is RM280.03 million for the Smallholder Oil Palm Replanting Financing Incentive Scheme (TSPKS) 2.0, followed by RM100 million for the Smallholder Farm Road Programme.
Another RM28.57 million is proposed for the Agro-Commodity Sector Disaster and Disease Control Fund, while RM17.05 million is proposed for downstream agro-commodity entrepreneurs.
The four areas address different needs — maintaining future production, improving access to farms, protecting crops and supporting businesses.
Why is replanting important?
Oil palm trees become less productive as they age, so replacing older trees can help maintain production, but newly planted trees take time before they start producing at useful levels.
For smallholders, replanting can also mean taking on the cost of clearing and planting again while waiting for the new trees to mature.
It also matters to the wider sector because maintaining oil palm production helps ensure there is enough supply for domestic processing and Malaysia’s export market.
Prime Minister Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim said the replanting programme would continue to help improve the productivity and income of smallholders in the long term.
Farm roads are crucial too

A farm road may seem like a very specific issue for people who do not live or work in plantations, but it can affect how produce is harvested and how equipment moves between farms, collection centres and mills.
A simple way to look at it is:
Oil palm fruit → collection → mill → processing → manufacturing → consumer or export market
Anwar, in his latest remarks, said the proposed farm road projects should provide basic infrastructure suited to plantation areas and directly improve smallholders’ productivity.
Does the price of commodities directly affect what we pay?
A change in the global price of palm oil or rubber does not automatically mean the price of a product on a supermarket shelf will change by the same amount.
Other costs are involved, including processing, packaging, transport, labour, exchange rates and business margins.
Government controls or subsidies can also affect the final price of some products.
For example, a rise in palm oil prices could increase costs for businesses that use palm-based inputs.
However, how much that affects the final price depends on the product and the other costs involved.
The same applies to rubber.
For example, a change in rubber prices can affect manufacturers, but it does not mean the price of a new set of tyres will immediately change by the same amount.
How do exports impact us?
The sector is not just about products used in Malaysia.
Malaysia also exports commodities and commodity-based products, bringing in foreign earnings and supporting businesses involved in processing, manufacturing, logistics and trade.

The commodity sector and commodity-based industries contributed RM19.65 billion to Malaysia’s GDP in the first quarter of 2026, while exports of commodity-based products generated RM41.62 billion during the same period, according to Noraini.
This is why what happens after commodities leave the farm also matters.
When more processing and manufacturing takes place in Malaysia, more economic activity can be generated locally before a product is sold here or exported.
What happens when production falls?
This is where replanting, disease control and measures to address climate-related disruptions are crucial.
If production of an important commodity falls, there may be less raw material for Malaysian processors and manufacturers.
Businesses could then face higher costs or have to look elsewhere for supplies, depending on market conditions.
For Malaysia, lower production can also affect the amount of commodities available for export and the earnings generated from them.
This is why some of the Budget 2027 allocation is focused on maintaining production and protecting crops, rather than only helping with immediate consumer needs.
So, how will Malaysians feel the impact?
The RM425.65 million proposed under Budget 2027 is not a direct payment to consumers.
For Malaysians, the impact could be seen through more productive smallholders, better movement of agricultural produce, stronger domestic processing and more resilient supply chains.
There is also a wider economic benefit if Malaysian companies can continue producing and exporting commodity-based products competitively.

So while the allocation may start with plantations and smallholdings, its effects can extend much further — to the products Malaysians use, the businesses that depend on these commodities and the exports that contribute to the economy.
8fd2dbfddb81a061: TORU-AYGYR (Kyrgyzstan), Oct 6 — The sun had barely risen, but diving volunteer Elizaveta Bodrova was already raring to plunge into the cold waters of Lake Issyk-Kul, where the ruins of a once-thriving city have lain submerged for centuries.

Situated on an ancient trading route between China and Europe, little is known about the history of the settlement under Kyrgyzstan’s largest lake or how it came to be flooded an estimated 800 years ago.
Together with a team of around 20 scientists, Bodrova is helping uncover its past, findings that could shape our understanding of the history of Central Asia and beyond.

“The visibility isn’t very good today, but I hope we’ll still be able to find the boundary of the settlement,” the 42-year-old told AFP with a smile, before hopping off a motorboat into the depths below.
The project, which began in 2024 and is funded by the Russian Academy of Sciences, is the first major exploration of the site since it was rediscovered in the 19th century.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->

A photograph shows artefacts discovered by the expedition members at the underwater site on the bed of Lake Issyk-Kul of what is identified by researchers as a submerged medieval city on the Silk Road in the settlement of Toru-Aygyr in Kyrgyzstan on September 22, 2026. Situated on an ancient trading route between China and Europe, little is known about the history of the settlement under Kyrgyzstan's largest lake or how it came to be flooded an estimated 800 years ago. The settlement is located at the heart of what was once the Silk Road, a trading route that linked China to the Mediterranean from the 2nd century BC until the mid-15th century. — AFP pic
‘Blind spot’
The settlement is located at the heart of what was once the Silk Road, a trading route that linked China to the Mediterranean from the 2nd century BC until the mid-15th century.
Although often associated with nomads, what is now Kyrgyzstan has been inhabited by multiple civilisations throughout its history, among them Turkic dynasties that traded between Europe and China.
“This is actually a blind spot in history, even though it is right in the centre of Central Asia,” expedition director Maxim Menshikov, who was steering the boat, said of the ruins.

“It is a very important chapter in the history of humankind, because it was the period that linked East and West during the Middle Ages. The Silk Road is not merely the history of a single region, it is the history of Eurasia as a whole,” he added.

The section of Silk Road that passed through the settlement during its existence is thought to have been under the control of the Karakhanids, a Turkic dynasty that controlled much of Central Asia from the 9th to early 13th centuries.
Researchers believe the city, the name and population of which are not known, may have covered up to five square kilometres (nearly two square miles).
Accurately dating the remains has been difficult.
But traces of two cemeteries discovered at the site suggest they were built during the early Islamisation of the region.
Among the discovered remains was a decorated public building, possibly a mosque, public bath or religious school.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->

Maxim Menshikov, archaeologist and the expedition director, and fellow colleagues inspect the finds discovered by divers at the underwater site on the bed of Lake Issyk-Kul of what is identified by researchers as a submerged medieval city on the Silk Road in the settlement of Toru-Aygyr in Kyrgyzstan on September 22, 2026. Situated on an ancient trading route between China and Europe, little is known about the history of the settlement under Kyrgyzstan's largest lake or how it came to be flooded an estimated 800 years ago. The settlement is located at the heart of what was once the Silk Road, a trading route that linked China to the Mediterranean from the 2nd century BC until the mid-15th century. — AFP pic
Like ‘Pompeii’
After several hours scouring the lakebed, the divers returned to dry land with their spoils: the remains of animal bones and pottery shards.

“The bones that have been found will enable archaeologists to determine their diet and age of the remains, as well as the diet of the people who lived in this region,” said Viktor Pozdnyakov, a diver and laboratory assistant on the expedition team.
“The pottery will enable us to date the finds and determine the approximate period more precisely. And, of course, to understand where it was produced, how and by what method,” the 22-year-old added.
Back at base, the artefacts are carefully preserved, catalogued and recorded.
Among those in better condition was a child’s chamber pot, known as a “tuvaq”.
“In fact, these are still in use today in Central Asia and the Caucasus,” said Menshikov, pointing to it as evidence of the daily life in the city.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->

Maxim Menshikov, archaeologist and the expedition director, and fellow colleagues inspect the finds discovered by divers at the underwater site on the bed of Lake Issyk-Kul of what is identified by researchers as a submerged medieval city on the Silk Road in the settlement of Toru-Aygyr in Kyrgyzstan on September 22, 2026. Situated on an ancient trading route between China and Europe, little is known about the history of the settlement under Kyrgyzstan's largest lake or how it came to be flooded an estimated 800 years ago. The settlement is located at the heart of what was once the Silk Road, a trading route that linked China to the Mediterranean from the 2nd century BC until the mid-15th century. — AFP pic
Although known to researchers since the 19th century, the site has only been systematically explored in recent years by Russian and Kyrgyz teams.
The researchers hope their work will improve understanding of Central Asian history.
“You could compare this research to that of Pompeii,” said Menshikov, referring to the largely preserved ruins of an ancient Roman city buried by an eruption of Mount Vesuvius in 79 AD.
“They had a highly developed civilisation and culture. And in an instant, nature simply destroyed it all,” he said.
What submerged the city under Issyk-Kul remains a mystery.

Among the theories is that the settlement sank to the bottom of the lake following a landslide, or that it was gradually flooded by a “tectonic dam” — a natural damming of a water body that could have occurred following an earthquake.
The probable cause was a “past seismic disaster,” said Andrei Strelnikov, a geologist with the Russian Academy of Sciences. — AFP
74cb9a438986f07a: WASHINGTON, Oct 6 — A month before the US midterms, Democrats are eyeing control of Congress — and the power to put President Donald Trump on the defensive for the rest of his term by investigating his administration and stalling his agenda.

The November 3 vote is shaping up as a verdict on one of the most turbulent presidencies in US history — and, by several measures, Trump goes into it less popular than any predecessor facing midterms in modern polling.

Americans will elect all 435 members of the House of Representatives and 35 of the 100 senators, alongside governors in 36 states. The election decides who controls the legislature — which passes laws, sets the budget and polices the White House.

Forecaster Decision Desk HQ gives Democrats a 75 per cent chance of winning the House, projecting a 234-201 majority. It rates the Senate a near coin flip, with Democrats narrowly favored to take it 51-49.
Control of the House alone would hand Democrats powerful committees and subpoena authority.

House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries has vowed to “hold the crooks accountable” and says that, in the majority, his party would move to reverse Trump’s tariffs, end US involvement in the Iran war and restore health insurance subsidies.
He has left the door open to a third Trump impeachment.
A Senate win would go further, letting Democrats block Trump’s judicial and cabinet nominees.
Economic pain

Trump has chosen to make the election about his record — a risky bet given polling showing his approval rating in the mid-to-low 30s, the lowest of his political career, with just 17 per cent backing his handling of the cost of living.
A Wall Street Journal survey found no president heading into the midterms had polled worse in its surveys dating to 1990.
Trump returned to power promising to tame inflation, which now stands at 3.4 per cent — higher than when he took office.
The conflict in the Middle East, now in its eighth month, has pushed gasoline above US$4 (RM16.34) a gallon. Only around a third of Americans approve of the strikes on Iran.
Republican Senate candidates in Iowa, Michigan and Ohio have publicly urged Trump to end the war.

And a sitting Republican senator called for investigations after the president’s eldest son received a lavish wedding gift from a Kremlin-linked Russian businessman — one of a string of Trump ethics controversies Democrats have folded into their pitch on affordability.
“The midterms could go down as one of the greatest self-inflicted political wounds in history,” said political analyst and former Senate aide Andrew Koneschusky.

“From the impact of tariffs to the Iran war, so much of the economic pain the American people are feeling, and the political pain Donald Trump’s party will likely feel in November, was entirely avoidable.”
Republican firepower
Yet the formidable cash advantage held by Republicans means a Democratic sweep is not certain.
Trump’s MAGA Inc super PAC entered September with US$416 million in the bank, and Republican groups are outspending Democrats on the airwaves in several key Senate races.
House Speaker Mike Johnson is touring more than 40 districts in the final stretch, offering voters what he calls “a clear choice between common sense and Democrats’ crazy.”
Congressional maps redrawn to protect incumbents have sharply cut the number of competitive seats, capping how far a historic wave of discontent can translate into seats.

A gain of around 19 House seats would fall short of the 27-seat average midterm loss for a president’s party over the past 90 years. It would be less than half the 40 seats Republicans lost in 2018, during Trump’s first term.
Still, the battlefield has widened since the summer. Democrats are now competitive in Senate races in Texas, Ohio, Iowa and Alaska — states Trump won by double digits in 2024.
For Trump, barred from seeking a third term, the midterms come just as the fight over his legacy, and over who inherits his movement in 2028, begins in earnest.
“A strong Republican showing would reinforce the argument that Trump permanently reshaped American politics,” political analyst Michael Fahey told AFP.
“Significant Republican losses would raise a very different historical question: Was Trump building a lasting political movement, or was Trump himself the movement?” — AFP
3c68ea991f83c133: BUENOS AIRES, Oct 6 — Lionel Messi will bring the curtain down on his glittering Argentina career on Tuesday with a farewell friendly against Benin that marks the dawn of a new era for the South American champions.

After more than two decades of service to his country, the 39-year-old superstar will hand over the captain’s armband for good as he makes his final appearance in the Albiceleste jersey at the Estadio Monumental in Buenos Aires.

Messi will be joined for his international swansong by 85,000 spectators and several of the teammates with whom he reached the pinnacle of football at the 2022 World Cup in Qatar, alongside members of Argentina’s emerging generation.
The friendly marks a symbolic passing of the torch for a player whose international legacy includes a World Cup title, two Copa America crowns and the Finalissima.
Messi also bows out as Argentina’s record appearance-maker and leading scorer, with 125 goals in 207 games, as well as a record 68 assists.
His farewell comes two and a half months after Argentina’s ill-tempered World Cup final defeat to Spain in New Jersey, where Messi exited in tears after making little impression.
“I gave it my all; I have nothing left to give, and besides, there are great young players coming up who deserve their chance,” Messi wrote when announcing his international retirement in August.
Messi remains under contract with Inter Miami until 2028, although following the death of his father, Jorge, two months ago, he revealed he may hang up his boots for good sooner than anticipated.
Friends reunited

Members of Argentina’s 2022 World Cup-winning squad — the players who delivered the country’s third star — and their families will join Messi for Tuesday’s farewell against Benin, ranked 93rd in the world.

Veterans of that Doha triumph such as Angel Di María, who retired from international football in 2024, will be there to witness the passing of the torch to a new generation charged with extending the Albiceleste’s golden era.

Several of the newcomers, including Franco Mastantuono and Leonel Flores, were not even born when “La Pulga” (“The Flea”) made his Argentina debut in 2005 for a team whose history had for so long been dominated by Diego Maradona.
“It’s going to be an unforgettable day for everyone. Everyone wants to be at this match, and now it’s just about enjoying it,” Argentina coach Lionel Scaloni said.

Argentina’s new generation has already shown what it can do without its captain, although nobody is pretending replacing a man regarded by many as the greatest footballer in history will be straightforward.
“Collectively, we will try to fill the void left by Leo,” said Scaloni, who is negotiating a contract extension after leaving his future unresolved following the World Cup defeat in July.
Scaloni, who mastered the art of building the right supporting cast around Messi, will also say goodbye on Tuesday to 38-year-old vice-captain Nicolas Otamendi.
Like Messi and Otamendi, midfielders Rodrigo De Paul and Giovani Lo Celso were called up solely for the Benin game, raising the possibility that neither will represent Argentina again.
New generation

Those certain to be involved, at least from the bench, include other veterans of the 2022 World Cup who will be the standard-bearers for Argentina after Messi: defender Cristian Romero, midfielders Alexis Mac Allister and Enzo Fernandez, and forwards Julian Alvarez and Lautaro Martinez.
Tenacious centre-back Romero is set to inherit the captain’s armband, first worn by Messi at the 2010 World Cup in South Africa.
Goalkeeper Emiliano Martinez and Lautaro Martinez are next in the captaincy hierarchy.
They have already begun to rally around Messi’s heirs, who showed their appetite for success in Argentina’s first game since the World Cup final, against Bolivia in Cordoba on Wednesday.
Argentina swept the Bolivians aside 4-0, with young talents Nico Paz and Jose Manuel Lopez among the scorers.
They followed that victory with a 7-0 rout of Burkina Faso at the Monumental on Saturday, with Mastantuono and Gianluca Prestianni scoring their first international goals.
While Argentina’s future is beginning to take shape, one small but symbolically significant question remains: who inherits Messi’s number 10 shirt?
“We won’t give the number 10 to anyone until Leo’s match takes place,” Scaloni said. “After that, we’ll see.” — AFP
8a7ed7e8c1974807: MACON, Oct 6 — Tierra Hollis fans herself with a sheaf of flyers in the late summer heat as she goes door-to-door in Georgia as part of the Black Voters Matter Fund’s push to fight alleged US disenfranchisement after recent electoral law changes.

“We get out here and we tell them their rights because the government might not always tell them,” said the 22-year-old, part of the organization’s efforts to make sure sweeping voting reform has not removed legitimate voters from rolls ahead of key midterm elections held on November 3.

Voting reform has become a flashpoint issue ahead of the election, with President Donald Trump insisting that laws need widespread changes to ensure election integrity, and rights groups arguing restrictive new laws are curbing voter access.
Trump has frequently alleged voter fraud since he lost the US presidential election in 2020, and Georgia was at the center of his unfounded claims.

In August 2023, an Atlanta grand jury indicted Trump and 18 others under racketeering laws on charges including that he called a senior official in the southern state and demanded that he “find” 11,780 votes needed to reverse his loss there in 2020.
The charges were dropped after Trump was re-elected for his second term.
Since 2021, US states have passed dozens of “restrictive” voting laws that cause voter suppression, according to the Brennan Center for Justice.
This year alone has seen nine states pass 12 such laws, the rights group says.

Since Trump’s election loss in 2020, Republican-led Georgia has enacted a slew of election reform laws that have tightened voter access by requiring additional forms of identification, narrowed access to absentee ballots and voting dropboxes and vastly expanded the scope of ways that anyone can challenge voter eligibility.

One of the oft-ridiculed clauses in the new Georgia laws makes it illegal to offer food or water to voters standing in long lines outside polling places — a regular occurrence in heavily-populated urban areas that have higher Black and working-class populations.
“All of this is to gain power. All of this is to keep Black and Brown people in our place,” Wanda Mosley, deputy policy director at Black Voters Matter Fund (BVMF), told AFP.

“I don’t have time to go back down to the county board of elections office with more ID when I’m probably working two jobs just to keep food on the table,” she added, explaining how mass voter challenges and additional requirements disproportionately hit working-class voters.

“I feel like the Republican Party has found itself in a situation where they want to go back to what this country was like pre-Reconstruction, pre-Emancipation,” she said, referring to a period in the 1800s when slavery was legal in the United States.
‘Fig leaf’
Republicans deny allegations that the laws target Black and working-class people, arguing that reforms were necessary to combat alleged voter fraud.
“I see this as being pro-America, pro-accuracy, pro-transparency and pro-election integrity,” Georgia lawmaker John LaHood said of one of the major electoral law changes when it passed.
The new laws also include more explicit rules for how ballots are handled and counted, mandate hand recounts in close races and require Georgia to move to a non-QR-code based system by 2028.
The latter is a key Trump demand that stems from unproven conspiracy theories that voting machines in areas where he lost were hacked to alter the results.

Noah Beck, the election director in Polk County responsible for his region’s 30,000 voters, says the voting machines are 100 per cent accurate, but that he is open to whatever changes are required to gain voter trust.
“I hate a world where election legislation is politicized because ultimately it is an objective goal that we all have is that we want safe and secure elections,” he said.

For Carol Anderson, a professor of African American Studies at Emory University, however, the argument that the reforms are needed to regain voter trust lost due to unfounded allegations is “pernicious.”
“It’s putting up these barriers, but it’s putting a fig leaf in front of these barriers, and that fig leaf is ‘election integrity,’” she told AFP.
“What actually is happening is it is trying to destroy democracy by removing American citizens from access to the ballot box.”
Back in Macon, one of Hollis’s colleagues out canvassing voters to make sure they make it to the polls is Octavia Brooks, a working-class grandmother.
“Back then, when my granny was coming up, she wasn’t allowed (to vote),” she said.
“That’s why people like me get out in the community, and we give example, and let them know it’s okay for you to voice your opinion.” — AFP
2cc21a3abc84d45d: From Moaz Nair

In multiracial Malaysia, authentic patriotism requires an objective, rigorous engagement with historical truths. To achieve this, secondary school curricula must prioritise critical inquiry over passive, uncritical acceptance.

For generations, history classrooms have functioned as secular chapels where students are expected to passively consume, memorise and venerate state-sanctioned narratives. While educators frequently assert that the primary goal of history education is to instil patriotism, a fundamental question remains unaddressed: what paradigm of patriotism is being cultivated?

A superficial patriotism built upon sanitised, heavily curated myths leaves a citizenry intellectually fragile. Conversely, a robust allegiance to the nation demands cognitive rigor – specifically, the academic courage to evaluate the past objectively through a critical lens.
Loss of historical nuance

Requiring students to accept textbook narratives without question does a disservice to both pedagogical standards and democratic citizenship. History is not a static ledger of undisputed facts; rather, it is a dynamic, ongoing dialogue between the past and the present, woven from the varied perspectives of both dominant and marginalised actors.

When school curricula reduce complex epochs to oversimplified, nationalistic narratives, they degrade a dynamic discipline into mere rote memorisation of dates and nomenclature. The deficiencies of this approach become evident when analysing the systemic omissions and oversimplifications within history textbooks.

A pertinent case study is the traditional pedagogical coverage of the 1875 assassination of J.W.W. Birch, the first British Resident of Perak. Students are conventionally taught that Birch was assassinated due to his interference with local customs, or adat Melayu.
Birch and debt slavery
However, curricula routinely omit the crucial, uncomfortable specificities of this interference: Birch’s aggressive campaign to abolish debt slavery.

By shielding students from this complex reality – wherein a colonial figure maintained a morally justifiable stance against human bondage while operating within a flawed imperialist framework – the curriculum privileges narrative convenience over historical accuracy.

This obfuscation of structural realities is indicative of a broader trend of presenting historical events in a unilateral vacuum. Prominent local historians note that in recounting the pivotal Pangkor Treaty of 1874, textbook narratives frequently replicate outdated colonial tropes, attributing British intervention strictly to internal royal disputes and secret society clashes.
Consequently, they obscure the crucial roles played by early capitalists who actively bankrolled and manipulated these regional factions to secure lucrative mining monopolies.
Structural amnesia

Beyond structural simplifications, recent curricular omissions risk fracturing national identity. Recent iterations of the secondary school syllabus have drawn sharp criticism from academics for downplaying the monumental economic and foundational contributions of Malaysia's plural society.

The exhaustive efforts of early Chinese and Indian communities in transforming the nation’s tin mining and rubber industries – alongside the significant loss of life during the construction of Malaya's foundational railway and road infrastructure – have been increasingly minimised compared to older editions.

Erasing the labour and sacrifice of minorities and indigenous groups from the master narrative implicitly signals to students that only select demographics contributed to the nation's state-building process.

Critical analysis of historical narratives within the pedagogical text exposes frequent contradictions, omissions and discrepancies. When scholars and students interrogate these reductive frameworks, they inevitably find that it presents a highly sanitised or biased rendering of the past.

These instructional flaws underscore the urgent need for a pedagogical shift from passive consumption to critical analysis. Teaching history through a critical framework involves training students to interrogate authoritative texts, cross-examine competing primary and secondary sources, and identify the ideological motivations underpinning historical documents.

Addressing “historical amnesia” requires unearthing the untold narratives of marginalised or uncomfortable perspectives, whether dealing with the harsh realities of colonialism, internal socio-political injustices or structural inequalities.
Civic engagement

Opponents of a critical historical framework often express concern that questioning established narratives will erode national pride. However, empirical observations suggest the opposite: institutional propaganda and state-sanctioned distortions breed civic cynicism.

In contrast, an evidence-based approach to history fosters deep civic engagement. When students are trusted to evaluate historical evidence, recognise systemic bias, and navigate the nuances of human conflict, they develop the vital analytical skills necessary to decipher propaganda and participate meaningfully in a pluralistic society.

If educators intend for students to contribute to an equitable future, curricula must move away from demanding the memorisation of a single, immutable story. Classrooms must equip students to participate in historical dialogue and independent critique.

True patriotism does not demand cognitive blindness regarding a nation's historical blemishes or cultural diversity; rather, it requires a comprehensive understanding of these elements to construct a more honest and inclusive society.

Educational institutions must confront the realities of the past. A transparent evaluation of historical trajectories is foundational to building an equitable future and inspiring authentic patriotism. Therefore, secondary history education must never devolve into an exercise in political indoctrination.

In an increasingly interconnected global information ecosystem, suppressing uncomfortable historical truths is an unsustainable strategy; inquisitive students and parents will inevitably uncover alternative narratives omitted from the formal classroom.

Ultimately, confronting an authentic past with an open mind does not divide a population; instead, it empowers a society to build a fairer future and fosters a deeper, more resilient love for the country.
Moaz Nair is an FMT reader.
The views expressed are those of the writer and do not necessarily reflect those of FMT.
9c94c1fc96a6d34c: SUBANG JAYA: Only a few letters separate “neurodivergent” from “neurotypical”. However, in everyday life, the distance between the children those words describe can feel much greater.

Special-needs teachers Sueveena Shalni, Kaminee Mahalingam and Nuha Damanhoori Hilal hope to bring these children closer through Giggles and Mess, a playgroup where they can meet, have fun and make friends.

“We want to create a safe space where kids who are neurodivergent and neurotypical can just be themselves, where we don’t restrict them by saying, ‘Oh no, you must do this, this and this.’ Just have fun,” Sueveena, 28, told FMT Lifestyle.

The idea is simple: for an hour-and-a-half to two hours, children participate in two or three activities, whether storytelling, arts and crafts or sensory play. Amid the fun, the trio hope the children will learn to understand one another.
“Neurotypical and neurodivergent children in the same space, communicating and showing kindness and love for each other. That’s what we want to achieve,” said Nuha, 27.

That starts by letting them play together without labels. “What we try to do from the start is avoid creating that separation, like saying, ‘Your friend is special and you are normal.’ We just start the session, and if they are curious, we explain nicely,” Sueveena said.
Kaminee recalled how a little girl once asked why another child was “a little bit different". The boy, who has non-verbal autism and is hard of hearing, uses an iPad to express himself.
“We helped her understand that it’s his way of communicating,” said Kaminee, 34.

That small exchange captured what they hope to achieve through Giggles and Mess, which the three colleagues started last November. They aim to hold one session a month, always on a Saturday, at different venues across the Klang Valley.
Each session has its own theme, such as “Winter Wonderland” to “Walking in the Jungle”, with two or three activities, breaks for rest and snacks and a goodie bag to take home.
The trio prefer outdoor spaces, where children have room to run around and enjoy some gadget-free time in the open air.

Parents pay for each session, which is capped at 10 children. The playgroup welcomes children aged three to nine, although older neurodivergent kids can join too. Children with cerebral palsy, autism, ADHD and those who are hard of hearing have attended.

At a recent playgroup attended by FMT Lifestyle, the children were seen enjoying an engaging storytelling session, making textured houses inspired by the film “Up” and exploring colourful sensory beads.
Beyond the fun, the activities also give children the chance to practise listening, communicating, following instructions and solving problems - skills they need in everyday life.
The teachers also run hands-on workshops where children have made fruit juice, milkshakes and even pasta from scratch. The trio organise birthday parties too.

Over time the children grow more comfortable in the group. Kaminee recalled a little girl who cried through her first few sessions and needed to be held. Now, she settles in quickly and enjoys herself.

Nuha cherishes the small breakthroughs that might be easy for others to miss. “Some neurodivergent children need a routine and can be a bit rigid about how things are supposed to be. Our playgroups can be a bit chaotic - we jump from one activity to another.
“But I’ve seen progress: they’re more comfortable with going with the flow instead of needing to know what comes next. They’re calmer when taking part in our activities,” said Nuha.
The trio’s long-term hope is to find a permanent space for Giggles and Mess.
For the teachers, every chance to play together is also a chance for children to learn how to make room for one another.
“These kids are going to grow up, become more aware and be part of society. So we hope that this can help create a more inclusive community,” Sueveena concluded.
Follow Giggles and Mess on Instagram, Threads and TikTok.

6f63da7502cea5ea: Krisis salah laku buli dan keganasan ekstrem dalam kalangan pelajar di institusi pendidikan negara kini menuntut resolusi yang matang dan menyeluruh, bukannya polemik politik yang tidak berkesudahan.

Rentetan insiden ngeri yang dilaporkan kebelakangan ini membuktikan bahawa isu tersebut bukan lagi sekadar pelanggaran disiplin biasa, sebaliknya telah berevolusi menjadi ancaman jenayah berat yang mampu meragut nyawa.

Malangnya, setiap kali tragedi seumpama ini meletus, tumpuan masyarakat sering kali tersasar. Amat tidak adil untuk menuding jari secara melulu dan meletakkan beban kesalahan sepenuhnya ke atas bahu warga pendidik.

Realitinya, dengan populasi pelajar yang begitu besar di seluruh negara, pihak sekolah berdepan cabaran luar biasa dalam mengekang penularan keganasan sistemik ini. Hakikat yang perlu ditelan ialah punca utama masalah ini jelas berakar umbi daripada kerapuhan institusi kekeluargaan itu sendiri.

Kebimbangan masyarakat kini berada pada tahap yang amat meruncing. Negara pernah dikejutkan dengan kes menyayat hati di Kuala Pilah, membabitkan seorang pelajar tingkatan dua yang meninggal dunia di asrama akibat dipukul oleh pelajar senior.

Keadaan menjadi lebih cemas apabila mayat seorang pelajar perempuan tingkatan empat ditemui dengan kesan kecederaan kejam di sebuah dewan sekolah di Yong Peng, Johor — kes yang membawa kepada penahanan tiga pelajar lelaki berusia 16 tahun.
Rentetan tragedi ini menjadi loceng amaran paling keras bahawa barah keganasan yang luar biasa sedang mengancam institusi pendidikan kita.

Namun, adakah adil jika hanya pihak sekolah dan guru dijadikan kambing hitam? Meletakkan tanggungjawab memantau dan memulihkan kecacatan tingkah laku jutaan pelajar setiap minit di atas bahu pihak pengurusan sekolah adalah satu jangkaan yang tidak realistik.
Kajian jelas menunjukkan bahawa kelakuan agresif, impulsif, dan kegagalan mengawal amarah dalam kalangan pembuli sebenarnya dibentuk oleh persekitaran domestik yang pincang.

Pengabaian emosi oleh ibu bapa, pendedahan kepada keganasan domestik, serta isu penyalahgunaan bahan dalam keluarga menjadi pemangkin utama. Golongan pembuli ini sekadar mengeksploitasi konflik dengan rakan sebaya di sekolah sebagai manifestasi daripada amukan toksik demi menuntut perhatian yang gagal diperoleh di rumah sendiri.
Situasi ini menjadi lebih parah apabila keganasan fizikal kini dipengaruhi oleh peranti digital tanpa sempadan. Majoriti ibu bapa kerap melaporkan anak-anak mereka pernah menjadi mangsa buli siber.

Modus operandi yang merangkumi ancaman kesat, penyebaran imej mengaibkan, dan kecaman terbuka di media sosial bertindak sebagai penderaan psikologi tanpa henti. Tindakan ini memusnahkan kestabilan mental mangsa.

Apabila kecelaruan emosi ini gagal dikawal, ia bukan sahaja mendorong mangsa bertindak balas membuli golongan yang lebih lemah, malah lebih tragis, ada yang mengambil jalan singkat membunuh diri akibat rasa tidak berdaya yang melampau.

Bagi memastikan krisis ini ditangani secara tuntas, pendekatan konvensional tidak lagi memadai. Kerajaan dan kementerian berkaitan perlu menguatkuasakan reformasi polisi serta perundangan yang lebih tegas dan holistik:

Penguatkuasaan Liabiliti Ibu Bapa (Parental Liability): Menggubal atau meminda perundangan domestik (seperti Akta Kanak-Kanak 2001) untuk mengenakan tindakan undang-undang atau denda berat ke atas ibu bapa yang dikesan melakukan pengabaian tegar sehingga anak-anak mereka terjebak dalam jenayah buli yang ekstrem.

Polisi Toleransi Sifar (Zero-Tolerance Policy) Standard: Mewujudkan garis panduan standard di peringkat Kementerian Pendidikan Malaysia (KPM) yang mewajibkan tindakan penggantungan atau pembuangan sekolah serta-merta terhadap pelaku buli tegar, tanpa sebarang kompromi politik atau cubaan melindungi reputasi institusi.

Pemantapan Penguatkuasaan Akta Keselamatan Siber: Mengetatkan kawalan dan mempercepat proses pendakwaan di bawah Akta Komunikasi dan Multimedia 1998 terhadap pembuli siber bagi menyekat penularan trauma digital.

Sistem Pelaporan Bersepadu Antara Agensi: Menyepadukan sistem laporan buli sekolah secara langsung dengan Polis Diraja Malaysia (PDRM) dan Jabatan Kebajikan Masyarakat (JKM) untuk memastikan tiada kes jenayah yang disembunyikan di peringkat dalaman sekolah atas alasan menjaga nama baik.

Pihak sekolah hanya mempunyai kapasiti untuk memberikan intervensi secara reaktif, seperti sesi kaunseling sokongan. Institusi pendidikan sama sekali tidak mampu merawat kerosakan tingkah laku yang akarnya sudah lama merebak dari ruang tamu rumah.

Untuk memutuskan rantaian epidemik keganasan ini, unit kekeluargaan wajib mengambil peranan utama. Ibu bapa memegang obligasi mutlak untuk menyemai daya tahan emosi serta membentuk disiplin anak-anak bagi memastikan mereka tidak menjadi pelaku mahupun sasaran jenayah buli.
Pertahanan terbaik anak-anak kita tidak bermula di pagar sekolah; ia bermula di rumah.
Moaz Nair adalah pembaca FMT.

c5ee96c0c3f18835: WASHINGTON: The US on Monday warned foreign financial institutions that if they conducted any business with Iran or its banking sector they could be sanctioned by Washington.

"Foreign financial institutions continuing to transact with sanctioned Iranian financial institutions could be targeted at any time without advance notification and should take immediate action to terminate such activity and relationships," the US Treasury said in an "alert" statement.
The United States launched its war against Iran in late February, killing the country's leadership and demanding it cease any nuclear-related activities.

The war has plunged the Middle East into violence, with Tehran's retaliatory action targeting Washington's Gulf allies and sending global energy and fertiliser prices skyrocketing after it virtually shut a key trading route.

Since late August, Washington has stepped up its campaign to economically isolate Tehran, warning its allies that they would be hit by secondary sanctions if they continued to conduct transactions with the country's government.
The US Treasury has also announced a slew of new sanctions as part of that push, targeting Iran's financial, crypocurrency, rail, automotive and manufacturing sectors.
It has also taken action against two banks - one in the United Arab Emirates and another in Turkey - over their alleged aid to the authorities in Tehran.

In Monday's statement, the Treasury said Iran's government operated so-called "shadow banking" channels to circumvent US sanctions, and that foreign financial institutions should aim to identify and avoid any such activities.
