0d50af4c771d5123: Schneider Electric's market cap has more than doubled in the past four years as the AI boom has driven unprecedented demand for datacenter power and cooling infrastructure. Now the French multinational is cashing in on its good fortunes to cement its place as a key provider of industrial power and datacenter infrastructure with the $22.6 billion acquisition of American industrial software company PTC. Founded in 1985, PTC made a name for itself developing software for computer-aided design, plus lifecycle management tools for industrial products and applications. The all-cash deal, announced on Monday, positions Schneider Electric to capitalize on the proliferation of datacenters used to train and serve AI models at scale. Since ChatGPT kicked off the AI arms race in late 2022, datacenter design and power requirements have changed considerably. Forty-kilowatt air-cooled racks have given way to 250kW liquid-cooled systems that need much denser power delivery and thermal management systems, all of which need to work together. In light of the growing complexity and supply chain challenges facing datacenter deployments, Schneider has made several strategic acquisitions which expanded its role in bit barn development. In late 2024, not long after Nvidia unveiled its first all-liquid-cooled rack designs, Schneider invested roughly $850 million on a 75 percent stake in Motivair, one of the leading producers of cold plates, rack manifolds, coolant distribution units (CDUs) and rear-door heat exchangers required to support the widespread adoption of liquid-cooled servers. The company is expected to acquire the remainder of Motivair sometime in 2028. As Schneider's role in the datacenter has grown, users of its kit have more products to manage across their lifecycles. Buying PTC expands Schneider's lifecycle management offerings and introduces key design capabilities to its offerings. PTC isn't Schneider's only datacenter-centric acquisition this year. Back in June, the company paid $3.1bn for industrial data operations vendor Cognite. Speaking to investors on Monday, Schneider CEO Olivier Blum suggested that owning PTC and Cognite would enable the company to inject software-defined automation into power systems early in their development, improving their efficiency in the process. Datacenters are one of Schneider's initial targets. "We believe that at the design stage, it is super important that you can help your customer to design both product, machine, processes and energy system. This is where we see CAD engineering as a very critical part of the portfolio," Blum said, according to a transcript of his remarks to investors. That's assuming of course that Schneider doesn't run into any regulatory hurdles along the way. The deal, Schneider's largest ever, isn't expected to close until late next year. ®
a08c041ff5c57b4e: PARIS: Michael Olise starred as France stormed back from behind to thrash Belgium 4-1 in the Uefa Nations League on Monday, while Italy continued their resurgence with victory over Turkey.

Dodi Lukebakio's first-half strike had Belgium on track for a first competitive victory over France since 1981, but Zinedine Zidane turned to his star-studded bench and the hosts produced a devastating late surge.
Les Bleus struck four times in the final 13 minutes to keep Zidane's unbeaten record as coach intact as France edged closer to a place in the quarter-finals.

Desire Doue equalised with a low shot from the edge of the box before Olise pulled the ball back for Rayan Cherki to put France ahead as the floodgates opened, with substitutes accounting for all of the hosts' goals.
Olise put the game to bed with a scruffy third goal before he grabbed another in stoppage time to round off a breathtaking turnaround.
"I think we played well at the end. The first half was difficult.. but we kept going and we're happy," Olise told TF1.
The Bayern Munich winger has been France's most influential player in the early stages of Zidane's reign, netting four times in his last three matches despite starting only once.
"It's a team effort. He (Zidane) brings his own ideas and we follow him. We've done well in these four games and we'll keep going," said Olise.
France hold a three-point lead over Italy in Group A1, with Belgium another point behind.
Zidane's team will complete their group campaign with games away to Italy and at home to Turkey next month.
Italy, who are rebuilding under Roberto Mancini, moved up into second place courtesy of a 3-1 win over Turkey in Bologna.
Gianluca Scamacca drilled Italy ahead only for Aral Simsir to level just after the hour.

b70d175101b3050d: WASHINGTON: President Donald Trump said Monday that the United States had withdrawn all B-1 bombers from a British airbase because of unspecified threats that he believed were linked to Iran.
Washington confirmed earlier that the bombers had left the RAF Fairford airbase – used by the United States to launch strikes on Tehran – even as the British government insisted the site was safe.
"There were some threats," Trump told reporters at the White House.
"And rather than tempting the enemy – we'll capture the enemy and beat the enemy, but why should we leave them there? So we moved them around a little bit, not very far."

Speculation has swirled about the incident since police were called to the base in southwest England on September 27 after a local farmer reported a group of men with several vans engaged in "suspicious" activity.
Despite a major counter-terrorism probe, five suspects arrested at the time and a British-Iranian national detained afterwards have all since been released on bail.
Investigators did not find any explosives in the vans, but "a quantity of petrol was recovered," according to counter-terrorism police.
Trump would not comment on a report that the threat involved attack drones, saying: "I can't tell you that but if they did they'll suffer greatly."
"We actually know the people that made the threat," said Trump, adding: "They would be linked to Iran."
UK INSISTS BASE SAFE
The Pentagon confirmed the redeployment on Sunday.
"We can acknowledge now that all US bombers that were deployed to RAF Fairford have re-deployed to their home stations in the United States," it said in a statement.
The statement noted that "operational security precluded us from confirming the movement of our assets and forces in real-time."
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Monday expressed "confidence in the security of all of our bases."

American facilities "theoretically could be threatened at any moment, and that's why there's so much security built around them," Rubio said, adding that Washington had worked with London on the investigation and "they couldn't be more cooperative."

Two US officials told the New York Times that the bombers were moved after commanders received new threats about an Iran-backed plot. One US official said the new information was part of the same threat warnings that surfaced three weeks ago, but the situation became urgent in the past 24 hours, the Times reported.
Asked whether the base was safe, UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham's official spokesman said: "Yes."
"We have tried and tested approaches to defend our bases around the country and throughout the world," he told reporters.
HEIGHTENED SECURITY
Speculation about the motives behind the incident ranged from terror threat to fuel theft, as energy prices in the UK hit record highs this week.
Burnham has said there were "strong indications that Iran played a part" in the incident, a charge rejected by Tehran.
Trump had previously rebuked British authorities for releasing the arrested men – all in their mid-20s – on bail.
Iran's embassy in London said it "categorically rejects and strongly condemns" speculation that Tehran was involved.
Adding to the mystery, British media reported that officers were alerted to the incident by one of the initial suspects, but police have not commented on the reports.
Security at the base had reportedly been heightened.
Britain gave Washington permission in March to use Fairford for "specific defensive operations into Iran," and US bombers and other planes have since been seen taking off and landing at the base.
Fairford is the only airbase on Britain's mainland used for this purpose.
The incident came after a farmer living in the village of Whelford, near the airbase, called the police after seeing three vans blocking a road and a group of masked men fleeing the scene.

bc25a570a71178c8: The adoption of AI agents in millions of organizations is creating new opportunities for attackers to make them take malicious actions, such as exfiltrating database contents and sensitive business and personal information.

In the past five months, Google and four other organizations—with little in common except for their use of AI agents—have acknowledged vulnerabilities that exploit one agent inside a targeted network to spread harmful instructions to other internal agents. The technique is a special form of prompt injection that targets not the LLM but a particular agent, such as one for translation or data analysis. Guardrails inside such agents, if they exist at all, are often lax and will send the instructions to other agents down the chain. Because the latter agent explicitly trusts the first one, it follows the directions.

Independent researcher Syed Anas Mohiuddin tested agents from organizations including Google, JP Morgan Chase, Weviate, Rapid7, the French government's interministerial digital directorate, and the US federal government. His proof-of-concept attacks exploit trust gaps in MCP, short for Model Context Protocol. The standard is one way AI apps and agents communicate with each other inside an internal network. KUALA LUMPUR: Malaysia has only about 27 years to prepare for "aged nation" status, far shorter than the transition period in several developed nations.

Economy Minister Akmal Nasrullah Mohd Nasir told the Dewan Rakyat that the short window gives the government limited time to prepare, compared with 115 years for France, 73 years for Australia and 69 years for the United States.
He said Malaysia became an "ageing nation" in 2021, when those aged 65 and above made up seven per cent of the population.

"Based on current projections, Malaysia is expected to reach 'aged nation' status by 2048, when the proportion rises to 14 per cent, and 'super-aged nation' status by 2060, when it reaches 20 per cent," he said.
"Our transition also presents unique challenges because our income levels are lower than those of developed nations when they underwent the same transition."

Akmal was responding to a question from Dr Zaliha Mustafa (PH-Sekijang) on the status of the National Ageing Blueprint 2025-2045 and the government's preparedness to address the challenges of an ageing society.
He said the shift would mean slower workforce growth, inadequate retirement savings and sharply higher demand for healthcare and elderly care.
Akmal added that the blueprint is undergoing final government review, while the White Paper on Preparation for Becoming an Aged Nation will be tabled during the current parliamentary session.
On Dr Zaliha's proposal for a district rejuvenation pilot zone in Sekijang, where 10.8 per cent of residents are aged 60 and above, Akmal said the government was willing to consider it.
He acknowledged that young people moving to major cities had accelerated ageing in some areas, and that urban management and recreational tourism planning for the elderly needed to be reviewed.

Responding to Salamiah Mohd Nor (PN-Temerloh) on the role of youth, he said the "silver economy" could create business and employment opportunities in elderly care, health technology and digital services.
He added that the Economy Ministry, the Statistics Department and relevant agencies were formulating indicators to measure the silver economy's contribution to gross domestic product.

5a9741e438a85bbf: The attackers just keep coming after Citrix NetScaler appliances, as both the feds and private security researchers warn that someone found - and has already exploited - yet another Citrix bug before it had a patch. This latest vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-88779, is a memory overflow bug that leads to denial of service attacks. It only affects NetScaler ADC and Gateway appliances configured as a SAML (Security Assertion Markup Language) service provider or identity provider, used for single sign-on authentication. Late Friday, amid exploitation reports, Citrix confirmed that it was investigating a “newly observed issue related to SAML authentication in customer-managed NetScaler deployments.” By Saturday night, the vendor released a security advisory for NetScaler ADC and NetScaler Gateway with patches, urging vulnerable customers to “install the relevant updated versions as soon as possible.” Citrix also posted a blog about the vulnerability, confirming that it has observed targeted attacks on unmitigated NetScaler deployments that can lead to denial of service. Citrix did not answer our questions about CVE-2026-88779 - including how many instances have been affected and what attackers are doing after exploiting the bug - but urged customers to "quickly apply" the fix to NetScaler instances. "We were recently alerted to a new issue that affects service availability for some NetScaler deployments," a Citrix spokesperson told The Register. "After we were alerted to this issue we immediately developed and published a mitigation while concurrently developing, testing and deploying a fix." On Sunday, the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) confirmed CVE-2026-88779 was under active exploitation and ordered federal agencies to patch the bug by Wednesday. While the new vulnerability is not technically related to the earlier eight CVEs finally disclosed by Citrix on September 27 - weeks after miscreants began abusing two of these security holes (CVE-2026-88772 and CVE-2026-88771) - watchTowr researchers told us they suspect it has been used to purposefully crash machines, making exploitation of CVE-2026-88771 faster. “This vulnerability is incredibly simple to trigger, with a single specially crafted request being all that is needed to knock an appliance offline,” watchTowr’s head of threat intelligence, Jake Knott, told The Register. “Exploitation is already occurring in the wild, and disrupting an authentication gateway can prevent legitimate users from accessing the services behind it.” WatchTowr reproduced the vulnerability on Friday, and Citrix credited the attack-surface management company along with Bishop Fox with helping it address the issue. “Citrix provides an indicator-of-compromise script that teams can run to check exposed appliances for signs of compromise, though a clean result is not definitive proof,” Knott said. “Security teams should prioritize appliances configured as a Gateway or AAA virtual server with SAML authentication enabled, and affected organizations should apply the fixed build or Citrix’s interim mitigation if an immediate upgrade is not possible.”®

d6ea00a1db48bc14: While OpenAI and Anthropic stoke fears over rogue agents, Canadian model dev Cohere promises enterprises a safer and more consistent experience. On Monday, the company said it revamped its North agent harness, which launched early last year, to improve collaboration, access control, token spend, and overall security of the platform. As you'd expect from an enterprise focused agent framework, Cohere's North 2 is designed to tie into existing knowledge bases and SaaS apps in order to automate various business processes. North 2 introduces a variety of features and functions that should be familiar to anyone who's used Claude Code or OpenClaw. Among them is the concept of skills, libraries, and automations. Skills are arguably the simplest, and are essentially standard operating procedures documenting how the agent harness should complete tasks. The skills are often generated by working with the agent to complete a task and then documenting which steps achieved the best results. With North 2, Cohere says that it has made it easier for these skills to be shared so that users aren't wasting time reinventing the wheel. Presumably, this should improve consistency by avoiding having the agent take different routes to achieving its goal, something that might miss key information or nuance. To facilitate the creation of new skills, North 2 also introduces the concept of automations, generic templates that can be customized using a drag-and-drop graphical interface, not unlike LangFlow, which we looked at earlier this year. Alongside skills and automations, Cohere's North 2 does something similar for shared knowledge and assets, which it calls libraries, to ensure that agents are working off of the same datasets. Finally, North 2 adds memory, a core feature of most modern agent harnesses, to ensure that agents can maintain context across multiple sessions. In some sense, these features are a bit like self-generating macros, but rather than being limited to Excel, they work across multiple applications and data sources. Sovereign AI remains a major talking point for Cohere, which says enterprises can deploy North 2 where they like and use their preferred models. If enterprises want to deploy the harness on-prem in an air-gapped environment, they can. If they prefer to run it in the cloud, that's also an option. Along with new features aimed at collaboration and automation, North 2 implements new guardrails designed to help enterprises get a handle on their token spend and access controls. Flow control functionality, meanwhile, promises greater visibility into which departments are hogging all the tokens, while access control functionality offers admins the ability to assign access control lists to various libraries and skills so that interns can't get their hands on proprietary data just because they asked for it. North 2 is only the latest in a slew of enterprise focused agentic AI platforms which have been rolled out over the last year. Essentially every major and minor cloud provider has introduced some kind of agent harness tailored to enterprise needs. The competition has only gotten hotter over the last few weeks as OpenAI, Meta and others have set their sights on the enterprise. ®

f6226cec61e1a2c5: Apple’s attempt to integrate AI into its various operating systems hasn’t been entirely well received, nor has the decision to make Apple Intelligence increasingly difficult to disable completely. Thankfully, the open source community has come to the rescue. A recently released open source tool called RemoveMacAI does pretty much exactly what it says on the GitHub-hosted tin: Aggressively rips Apple Intelligence out of macOS, disabling most of its AI features and removing downloaded models following the launch of macOS 27 last month. Siri AI? Gone. ChatGPT and other AI extensions? Eliminated. Genmoji, random boxes offering to jazz up your writing, summaries of notifications and app content, and automatic photo clean-up? Never to be seen again. More importantly, RemoveMacAI can claw back the storage occupied by Apple’s AI models - potentially over 12 GB, depending on the Mac. You might just get confused and think it’s 2025 again. The impetus for RemoveMacAI, its creator Om Lahorey said in a LinkedIn post, is the fact that Apple made it practically impossible to remove Apple Intelligence features in macOS 27. “The settings are spread across about a dozen places, some of them only under Screen Time,” Lahorey wrote over the weekend. “Even with every one turned off, the models stay on disk. I wanted it gone in one step, so I wrote RemoveMacAI.” Unsurprisingly, Lahorey’s tool blew up on Hacker News, with plenty of people happy for an easy way to get rid of Apple AI tools. As of writing, the repo has over 1,500 stars, so it's clearly struck a nerve with frustrated macOS users. It’s simple to run, as its GitHub page explains: install it via a curl command to its GitHub repo, or with Homebrew, and then fire it up in the terminal. Selected features can be left enabled, or Apple Intelligence can be disabled completely, while a single command can revert the changes and restore the previous settings. RemoveMacAI works by installing a configuration profile, which the user has to approve, that applies Apple’s own restriction keys for Apple Intelligence features. Models are then removed via Apple’s asset service. Lahorey credits another open source tool called pared, and its developer, with mapping the asset service, model sets, and settings keys needed to remove Apple Intelligence. Pared functions similarly to RemoveMacAI – you can consider RemoveMacAI to be a more user-friendly wrapper for the other tool. As for whether it will persist, Lahorey explains that the config profile RemoveMacAI installs redirects the download for Apple Intelligence models to a closed local port, so updates to macOS shouldn’t result in the models being reinstalled. Also worth mentioning, Apple System Integrity Protection remains enabled with the models disabled and uninstalled, as no files under System are directly modified by the tool. Dictation should still work as well, as speech models aren’t removed by RemoveMacAI. That said, it’s certainly possible a future macOS update will break RemoveMacAI’s functionality. So if you’re interested in giving the tool a shot, there’s no guarantee this particular escape hatch will remain open forever. ®

3c9bc6c4f4c7545c: Over decades of research, scientists have built up a partial picture of what specialized cells within the brain and spinal cord do. By studying how the brain develops, they could identify genes that were active in different populations of neurons and where in the brain those neurons resided. In some cases, these genes could then be used to genetically delete the neurons, allowing us to get some indication of what they might be doing, building on the information we've obtained from studies of brains with damaged regions.

But this approach has its limits. The brain is flexible enough to potentially adapt to the loss of some cells, and their loss early in development may alter the development of any neurons they would have normally formed connections with. It would be far more informative to activate and shut down the neurons in an otherwise intact brain.

Today's Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine rewards three people—Karl Deisseroth, Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel—who developed our ability to do precisely that. Starting from studies of single-celled algae that are attracted to light, these and many other researchers built an entire field of study that we now call optogenetics: using light to alter the behavior of nerve cells marked by the activity of individual genes.

a692947f406514be: Microsoft Windows 11 26H2 has arrived, and, unfortunately, it's already picked up a known audio issue within weeks of release. The glitch also affects Windows 11 25H2 and 24H2, which share the same code branch. It relates to decoding AC-3 (Dolby Digital) audio and can cause the application using the decoder to crash abruptly or fail to start at all. Identified after the September 22 Windows update, the issue mostly impacts older applications, according to Microsoft. "Many modern applications do not use Windows for this type of encoding and therefore will not encounter this issue. "The code component involved in this issue is most commonly used in legacy applications that still rely on Windows built-in audio decoding." In summary – if your app has the temerity to use Windows built-in audio decoding for AC-3, you might have a problem. If it includes its own audio decoding component, you should be okay. "Affected applications may vary," explained Microsoft, "and can include games, media players, and certain productivity applications." There's also no fix as yet, so uninstalling is the only way to address it for now. To be clear, the AC-3 malfunction is not specific to Windows 11 26H2; the update preceded the release of the operating system's latest version by a week. It joins other known issues in 26H2, including other ongoing audio woes that have lingered in the list despite workarounds being available from Microsoft Support for Business. Microsoft currently has no mitigation for the AC-3 bug and offers little comfort to affected users: "We are working on releasing a resolution for this issue in a future Windows update." Acknowledging the latest trouble continues a run of misfortune for Microsoft. September's Patch Tuesday resulted in an out-of-band update to deal with RDP and Hyper-V issues. The update did not, however, fix all the audio problems it introduced, and the September 22 preview update has compounded the situation. Microsoft did not provide a timeline for resolving the latest issue. ®

7b441ca2abc39395: Sam Altman-backed AI chip startup Volantis has a plan to break through the memory wall using light, and this time it's not just an IP play. Founded in 2022, the San Francisco-based startup is developing an AI accelerator that will use a photonic interposer to dramatically increase memory bandwidth without compromising on capacity. Volantis believes it can pack upwards of 10 TB of memory at speeds up to 240 TB/s onto a single massive package. This, it claims, should be enough to serve a 20 trillion parameter model at 10,000 tok/s per user. To do this, Volantis is taking a somewhat unusual approach. Rather than developing some novel compute architecture or memory technology, the company is focusing its efforts on the optical interposer. Everything else it plans to license from IP providers. "The differentiation is primarily coming from the optical interposer. So why don't we license absolutely everything we possibly can, even if it's not the highest performance in the world, because we're already biting off a lot of risk with the interposer and the integration," CEO Tapa Ghosh tells El Reg. The basic idea behind the chip, which Volantis is calling A-1, is that by using optical wave guides rather than electrical interconnects it can dramatically increase the amount of high-bandwidth memory per package. Because of the speeds at which most AI accelerator memory, like HBM, operate, and the size and number of data pins used, it needs to be as close to the compute as possible to minimize power consumption and maximize signal integrity. As a result the maximum capacity and bandwidth of modern GPUs is limited by the compute die's shoreline. That's the physical perimeter around the chip. For now, that means the cap is right around 432 GB on AMD's MI455X. Photonic interconnects can extend that much farther. Instead of a few millimeters the memory can be located a few centimeters away, eliminating the shoreline as a bottleneck. While HBM is useful as an example, we'll note Volantis hasn't said what memory tech its chip will use just yet. Volantis aims to achieve this using optical waveguides integrated into an interposer. Compute and memory designed or supplied by its partners will be packaged on top. If any of this sounds familiar, Volantis isn't the first to propose using silicon photonic interposers in this manner. As our sister site Next Platform has previously reported, both Lightmatter and Celestial AI have toyed with the idea in the past. In fact, we strongly suspect the idea of HBM-at-a-distance contributed to Marvell's decision to acquire Celestial for $5.5 billion. However, unlike either Celestial or Lightmatter, Volantis isn't trying to license its tech to other chipmakers. At least not yet. Instead it aims to develop a fully fledged inference chip. "It is, at least on day one, a way easier problem to demonstrate a solution that ships," Ghosh says. Another differentiator is the technology on which the startup's interposer is based. Rather than relying on external lasers, Volantis' design uses micro vertical-cavity surface-emitting lasers — micro-VCSELs for short — and means the light source is integrated directly into the interposer. VCSELs aren't new by any means, but have faced criticism over their reliability. However, Volantis CTO Roy Meade tells us the technology has come a long way in recent years and by giving up some speed, significantly higher reliability can be achieved, a philosophy he describes as wide and efficient. "People are still constrained to this, what I would call a fat pipe point-to-point mentality, and naturally, if that's the case, you're going to go towards SerDes," he says. "If we were to go back and take a look at the benefits of a wide-and-efficient approach. HBM for example. Taking that same playbook makes a lot of sense." What Meade is getting at is that interconnects can achieve higher bandwidth in a couple different ways. The first is by increasing the link speed, and the second by using more links. For example an 800 Gbps link can be achieved using four 200 Gbps links or eight 100 Gbps links. In his example of HBM, higher bandwidth is achieved by using an extremely-wide bus but slower data rate per pin relative to other memory technologies. The same concept applies to Volantis' optical interposer-based accelerator. Power efficiency remains an open question that's dogged many photonics startups, but this may be less of a problem for Volantis because it's not trying to license its first-gen interposer tech. For its first product the company is targeting 1 picojoule per bit per 24 Gbps lane and a total system power of around 20kW. Volantis still has a ways to go before it tapes out its first production-ready chip, and will need to raise a fair bit more in venture capital to do that — far more than the $88 million it raised this week with the help of Lachy Groom, Abstract Ventures, and others. Ghosh is well aware of this. He says the funding will enable the company to scale from small-scale optical demonstrators to something more closely resembling the final product. The interposer alone is challenging enough, but then there is the complexity of actually integrating the IP they license. "Aggressively, we should aim for an MVP product in 12 to 18 months as our target," he tells us, noting that's to have a working prototype not volume production. ®

932d242f1548c95c: Well, it’s safe to say no Bahrain Grand Prix has been affected by torrential rain quite like the 2026 race.

For one thing, it was held several thousand miles from Bahrain itself. The ongoing war with Iran ruled such things out, so the Sepang International Circuit in Malaysia stepped in to fill its spot. One of the best examples of a late-'90s “Tilke track”—named for its designer, Herman Tilke—it’s characterized by a couple of long straights and the always-brutal tropical weather that provides one of the toughest physical challenges on the calendar. And this weekend was no exception.

Heavy rain arrived about half an hour before the start time, delaying things significantly. Although the sport has two different kinds of treaded tires for use in the rain, the full wet tire generates so much spray, and such slow lap times, that it's essentially only useful for circulating behind the safety car. d2e4790c9fabcfed: For all the data that AI systems continually amass and analyze, enterprise AI agents often suffer from a curious shortcoming: a lack of knowledge. More than data, knowledge is the understanding of what the data means in the context of individual organizations. AI agents need this understanding to reason about situations, make decisions, and ultimately take actions. Without sufficient knowledge, agents are prone to making flawed and unreliable decisions.

A lack of knowledge, our research finds, is a major reason agentic AI use cases never make it to production. Competitive pressure is making it urgent to address this. Organizations need to deploy and scale more of their agentic projects to capture the efficiency gains AI promises. Falling short risks wasting the investment already sunk into these projects, and it cedes ground to rivals already putting their agents to work more effectively.

The purpose of this report, which is based on a survey of 300 data, AI, and other technology executives, is threefold. First, it seeks to gauge organizations’ agentic knowledge capabilities (i.e., their ability to give AI agents a full contextual understanding of the data they ingest) across semantic knowledge, episodic memory, and procedural knowledge.

Second, the report probes the challenges organizations face in improving access to knowledge and ultimately to getting more agent use cases into production. Third, it explores the measures organizations are taking to overcome these challenges.
The key findings include the following:

Data and knowledge weaknesses consistently stall AI agent progress. On average, only around a third (34%) of organizations’ agentic AI projects make it into production. Even high-tech firms struggle with this. Legacy data systems, security and privacy concerns, and a lack of knowledge and context are the key points of failure.

Strong knowledge capabilities correlate with agent success. A small group of production leaders (organizations where on average 61% of agentic projects advance beyond pilot) have stronger knowledge capabilities than the rest, especially when it comes to semantics. This advantage tracks closely with their higher production rate.

Fragmented data hugely complicates knowledge access. Data fragmentation (the inadequate sharing of data across systems) was most commonly cited as a top challenge to expanding agents’ access to knowledge (cited by 55%). Production leaders, by contrast, are more likely to see security and privacy concerns as a major concern (cited by 72% of this group).

Most firms aim to strengthen the link between data and agents. Among steps that can yield higher quality agent decisions, executives expect the biggest impact to come from strengthening the structural foundation between the organization’s data and its AI agents. The experts we interviewed see a knowledge layer as a prime way to achieve this.

Investment priorities to boost knowledge range from pipelines to knowledge graphs. To expand agent access to knowledge, organizations will prioritize investments in retrieval technologies, like ingestion pipelines, AI-ready APIs, and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG); in AI evaluation agents; and in knowledge graphs.

1469bd84211a39cb: The age of LLM-assisted security vulnerability discovery is really starting to bite. Debian's latest Linux kernel security update comes with a formidable reading list of 1,313 CVE identifiers. The DSA-6528-1 Linux security advisory, published on September 29, covers kernel package version 6.12.111-1 for Debian 13, codenamed Trixie. Debian 13.7 was released on September 12, before upstream kernel 6.12.111 arrived nine days later. The Debian security tracker links to descriptions of the individual issues. We have not examined every entry. If we had, this article would not appear until after Debian 13.8 (which is likely to appear later in October), or possibly at some point in 2027. Several checked at random also affect older kernel versions, so the list should not be read as a tally of bugs introduced in 6.12.111. The Linux kernel project became a CVE Numbering Authority (CNA) in February 2024. Back in February this year, kernel maintainer Greg Kroah-Hartman described the Linux CVE assignment process in some detail. He said kernel development averages around nine changes an hour, with a feed of known bug fixes averaging about 30 changes a day providing the basis for the CNA team's review. The kernel team's policy is to assign CVEs automatically after fixes have reached a stable kernel tree. It takes a deliberately cautious approach because the security implications of a bug may not be apparent when it is fixed. A CVE identifier alone therefore says little about severity or exploitability. We strongly suspect that this number of CVEs is due to LLM bots doing the bug hunting, and quite possibly doing the bug fixing as well. Linux is not an anti-AI project, and neither is Debian. AI-assisted bug hunting is already swamping the Linux security mailing list, as The Register reported in May. Kroah-Hartman released kernel 6.12.112 on October 3. Its detailed changelog runs to more than 27,000 lines. With both the rates of change and the sizes of the changes getting so large, it is hard to deny that LLM bot assistance must be very useful to the hard-pressed maintainers. Whether coding bots constitute a net benefit to the projects, to software, or to humanity as a whole remains at best an open question. ®

1d28d12072be0171: In 2026, the question for enterprise AI is no longer whether predictive models can outperform statistical forecasts—that argument is settled. The big question now is how to enable predictive systems to act on their own conclusions without drifting from business intent. The frontier has moved from prediction to autonomous decision making, and the gap between leaders and laggards is widening accordingly.
“Enterprises are done with a backward-looking point of view; they want to be more forward-thinking,” says Vishal Gupta, partner at research firm Everest Group.

Intelligent analytics, powered by technologies like deep learning and generative AI, are making this possible. Real-time training allows AI to evolve continuously instead of waiting for quarterly refreshes. In addition, the data that newer predictive engines rely upon has expanded to encompass not just neat, numerical records but also messy, unstructured sources of insight-rich interactions. As a result, AI-powered analytics are moving enterprises from passive hindsight to pragmatic foresight.

AI takes predictive analytics—a broad discipline that includes predictive modeling, data prep, analysis workflows, interpretation of results, and decision-making applications—to new heights. “In many ways I think the word ‘analytics’ is giving way to AI,” says Gupta. “Everything is becoming AI.”

b57368bb9d2a0ad6: STOCKHOLM, Oct 5 — Since 1901, the Nobel Prizes have been awarded to individuals and organisations for work leading to great advances for humanity, in line with the wishes of the prizes’ founder, inventor Alfred Nobel.
The 2026 winners will be announced between October 5 and 12, starting with the Nobel Prize in Medicine on Monday from 11:30 am (0930 GMT).
Here are five things to know about the prizes and their founder.
In detention
Since 1901, five Nobel Peace Prize laureates have been prevented from attending the awards ceremony in Oslo.
In 1936, German journalist and pacifist Carl von Ossietzky was detained in a Nazi concentration camp.

Myanmar opposition leader Aung San Suu Kyi was under house arrest when she won the prize in 1991. Given permission by the junta to travel, she declined for fear of potentially not being able to return to her country.
In 2010, Chinese dissident Liu Xiaobo was in prison. His chair remained empty, where the prize was placed.
In 2022, Belarusian human rights campaigner Ales Bialiatski was in jail. He was represented by his wife Natalia Pinchuk.
In 2023, Iranian activist Narges Mohammadi was held in Iran’s Evin prison when the prize was awarded.
Young and old
In 2014, 17-year-old Pakistani human rights activist Malala Yousafzai became the youngest winner of a Nobel Prize.
Another unusually young laureate was Australia’s Lawrence Bragg, who won the Nobel Prize in Physics jointly with his father in 1915 when he was 25, for work carried out at the age of 21.
Iraqi activist Nadia Murad was also awarded the Nobel Peace Prize at the age of 25 in 2018 for her efforts on behalf of the Yazidi minority.

In contrast, American John Goodenough was the oldest to become a Nobel laureate. He won the Prize in Chemistry in 2019 at the age of 97 for his work on the lithium-ion batteries that power smartphones and electric cars.
The year before, his compatriot Arthur Ashkin was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics at the age of 96.
Posthumous awards
Since 1974, the statutes of the Nobel Foundation stipulate that the prize may not be given posthumously.
But the prize may still be awarded if the recipient dies between the time of the announcement in October and the formal prize ceremony in December.
Before the change, only two people had won a Nobel Prize posthumously.
One was Dag Hammarskjold, the Swedish secretary-general of the United Nations, who died in a plane crash in 1961 but was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize later the same year.
And in 1931, the Nobel Prize in Literature was awarded posthumously to another Swede, poet Erik Axel Karlfeldt.
In 2011, the committee for the Nobel Prize in Medicine selected Ralph Steinman of Canada, unaware that he had passed away just three days before the announcement.
The foundation nevertheless gave him the award.
Women laureates
Only 68 of the 633 Nobel prizes awarded since 1901 have been given to women, representing about 10 percent, though the share has been steadily increasing since the early 2020s.

The science fields have the lowest representation of women laureates. The various committees that award the prizes have repeatedly refused to introduce quotas, instead encouraging nominations of women scientists.

Only five women have won a Nobel physics prize out of a total of 230 laureates in the discipline, three out of 99 economics laureates, eight out of 200 chemistry laureates, and 14 out of 232 medicine laureates.
Marie Curie was the first woman laureate in 1903 and she is to this day the only woman to have received two Nobel prizes, first for physics in 1903 and then in 1911 in chemistry.
Nobel the poet
Nobel went down in history as the inventor of dynamite but he also loved English poetry and was an admirer of Percy Bysshe Shelley and Byron.
He wrote poetry himself his entire life, sometimes in his native Swedish but mostly in English.
In a letter to a friend, he wrote: “I have not the slightest pretension to call my verses poetry; I write now and then for no other purpose than to relieve depression, or to improve my English.”
In 1862, at the age of 29 and questioning his literary talent, he sent a letter in French to a young woman that said: “Physics is my field, not writing.”

In 1896, the year of his death, he wrote a scandalous tragedy in four acts titled “Nemesis”, inspired by Shelley’s play “The Cenci” about a woman in 16th-century Rome who murders her incestuous father. — AFP

It was strange, new territory. Asking someone where they went to school is often not an innocent question. It is a way of “placing” you on a social scale. As thousands of freshers settle in to their first terms at university, a significant proportion will be battling with this dawning awareness that Britain runs on a network of private schools whose alumni often seem to know, or know of, one another. State-school students might have been dimly aware of it before, but nothing puts it into sharper focus than freshers’ week. It’s clear that little has changed since my own student days. I was saddened to read recent reports of classism at St Andrews, which led to a student’s announcement that she would not return this academic year: “Working-class students have been made to feel ashamed of their home life at university,” she said. The pervasiveness of private school culture, as I suppose you could call it, remains nationwide and deeply embedded. Rhiannon Lucy Cosslett is a Guardian columnist Continue reading...

6db01a0f6cd36cc1: This is today’s edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology.

be22f622e0667395: KUALA LUMPUR, Oct 5 — Recovering funds linked to the procurement of missiles for the Littoral Combat Ship (LCS) will not be resolved immediately and will take time, Defence Minister Datuk Seri Mohamed Khaled Nordin said.

7bb178406108f4bc: STOCKHOLM, Oct 5 — The Nobel medicine prize was awarded Monday to US psychiatrist and neurologist Karl Deisseroth and German scientists Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel for their pioneering work in the field of optogenetics.
Optogenetics involves controlling nerve signals with light, and helps researchers understand how specific cell types contribute to behaviours like learning, fear, addiction and movement.
The trio were honoured “for their discovery of a molecular switch for nerve cells”, the Nobel Assembly said.
Using light, researchers are now able to switch individual neural circuits on or off in a brain.
They have been able to reveal neural circuits governing specific memories, feelings, and behaviours relevant for neurological and psychiatric disorders.

In clinical medicine, the method is being used in attempts to restore sight in people with visual impairment, and may one day lead to treatments for disorders such as Parkinson’s disease and epilepsy.
“Optogenetics provides opportunities for mapping the brain in a way that we could once only dream of,” Per Svenningsson, chair of the Nobel committee, said in a statement.

“Optogenetics has fundamentally altered our understanding of the brain. Every day brings new discoveries, helping to solve one of humanity’s great mysteries: how our incredible brain works,” the Nobel Assembly said.
The secretary general of the assembly, Thomas Perlmann, told reporters he was able to reach the three laureates by phone to break the news.
“That was great to talk to them. I first called Deisseroth, he was very tired when he answered. He was definitely asleep, but he woke up,” he said.
Illumination
In the early 2000s, Hegemann and Nagel were examining why a single-celled alga was able to swim toward a light source.
They discovered an algal protein with unique properties, called channelrhodopsin, found on the surface of the cell.
When illuminated by blue light, a channel opens through the protein.
Charged ions then flow into the cell, creating an electrical impulse. They found that any cell they put the protein in became light sensitive.
Deisseroth then introduced the gene for channelrhodopsin into nerve cells from rats.
By illuminating the cells with blue light, he was able to trigger a nerve signal.
He published his breakthrough in 2005, and two years later, made the light-controlled switch for nerve cells work in the brains of living mice.
In 2021, Deisseroth and Hegemann won the Lasker Prize for their work in the field, often considered a precursor to the Nobel.
Deisseroth, 54, is a professor at Stanford University in the US, while Hegemann, 71, is a neuroscience professor at Humboldt University of Berlin.
Nagel, 73, is a biophysics professor at the University of Wurzburg.
The Nobel prize for physics will be announced on Tuesday, followed by the chemistry prize on Wednesday and the literature prize on Thursday.
Some pundits have suggested that for literature, the Swedish Academy could follow up last year’s award to Hungary’s Laszlo Krasznahorkai with a woman writer, possibly from Central or Latin America.
Argentine author Samanta Schweblin, 48, could be one such pick, literary critic Lina Kalmteg told AFP.
All eyes on peace
Perhaps the most keenly anticipated award is that due on Friday, the peace prize — the only Nobel to be awarded in Oslo.
This year, some experts have suggested the jury could choose a laureate who enjoys broad consensus, after last year’s winner, Venezuelan opposition leader Maria Corina Machado, stirred controversy.

Among possible laureates this year are a joint prize to Save the Children and Mykola Kuleba, a Ukrainian children’s rights activist campaigning for the return of Ukrainian children illegally taken to Russia from occupied territories.

Others include Sudan’s Emergency Response Rooms (ERR), a vast network of volunteers risking their lives to help people facing the double threat of war and hunger, and the Committee to Protect Journalists (CPJ) after the deadliest year on record for the profession in 2025.
The economics prize wraps up the Nobel season on October 12.

This year’s laureates will receive their prizes — a diploma, a gold medal and a US$1.2-million (RM4.9 million) cheque — on December 10, the anniversary of the death in 1896 of the prize’s creator, scientist Alfred Nobel. — AFP

81b8c09448309bbb: TAIZ, Oct 5 — Yemen’s military backed by Saudi jets attacked Houthi targets on Monday as they launched an ambitious campaign to recapture all territory from the Iran-backed group after its lightning gains during the Middle East war.
The military said it carried out more than 1,000 strikes, while 100 warplanes attacked at dawn, according to the Saudi-led coalition that supports Yemen’s government.
Yemen’s government announced the lofty goal of retaking all Houthi territory — much of it held for more than a decade — on Sunday.
Last month the Houthis seized swathes of coastline along the Red Sea and Bab al-Mandab strait, a chokepoint for oil and cargo shipping.

As the offensive began, a source in the Saudi energy sector told AFP that an attack on Sunday had again halted pumping in the East-West pipeline to the Red Sea, a key conduit since Iran blockaded the Strait of Hormuz.
The long-running conflict in Yemen, one of the world’s poorest countries and neighbour of Saudi Arabia, has flared anew months into the Middle East war that has sent crude prices soaring.

Saudi Aramco chief executive Amin Nasser warned on Monday that global oil stockpiles are “scarily thin” owing to the US-Iran war, days after G7 nations agreed to release more of their inventories to ease supply concerns.
“The system is already straining,” Nasser told the Energy Intelligence Forum in London. “And with precious little else the world can turn to, the supply resilience cushion is scarily thin.”
The Houthis have targeted Saudi oil infrastructure and tankers in the Red Sea since a ceasefire in Yemen’s civil war unravelled in July.
The group has accused the Saudi-led coalition of carrying out hundreds of strikes.
‘Stay and die’

A day after the new offensive was declared, Yemen’s military spokesman announced over 1,000 “strikes against artillery and rocket launcher positions, defensive fortifications, approach and reinforcement routes, supply lines and logistics assets, combat reinforcements”.

Coalition spokesman Major General Turki al-Maliki said 100 jets flew at daybreak as part of “Operation ‘Dawn of Yemen’“. They provided “round-the-clock air support for the Yemeni armed forces on the ground”, he wrote on X.
The strikes have yet to blunt ongoing Houthi advances on the ground.
On Sunday, the group effectively encircled the key city of Taiz after cutting the main supply route linking the city to the interim government capital of Aden.
However, Taiz residents remained defiant, vowing to stay and defend their city.
“We cannot leave the city. It is impossible for us to leave. We will stay and die inside this city,” Fahmi Ahmed Ghaleb told AFP.
“Throughout the earlier clashes with the Houthis, we also stayed inside the city.”
Humanitarian crisis
Taiz city remains under the control of government forces but has long been encircled from the north, east and west by Houthi fighters and remains one of the main fronts in Yemen’s war.

The Houthis’ surrounding of Taiz “is a significant development, but I think it is still too early to say that we are witnessing a decisive turning point”, Ahmed Nagi, a senior analyst for Yemen at the International Crisis Group, told AFP.
While the war in Yemen predates the Middle East war that began with US-Israeli strikes on Iran, it has become the most active front in the wider conflict in recent weeks.
The Houthis launched a rapid offensive around the Red Sea coast in September that killed hundreds of combatants on both sides and, according to UN figures, displaced more than 145,000 people.
The Houthis took control of Yemen’s capital, Sanaa, in September 2014, forcing out the internationally recognised government. They hold much of Yemen, including its most populous areas.

The Saudi-led international military coalition intervened in March 2015. The ensuing civil war caused hundreds of thousands of deaths and a spiralling humanitarian crisis that left a majority of the population relying on aid. — AFP

19d891c24d0ba926: KUALA LUMPUR, Oct 5 — Safety issues in schools should not be concealed to protect reputations, as this may prevent authorities from taking action, said Inspector-General of Police Tan Sri Mohd Khalid Ismail.

b43000d93607564d: Ubuntu 26.10, “Stonking Stingray,” has entered beta testing, slightly later than planned – it is in fact scheduled to be released on October 15. While many people will stay with the LTS version, there’s some interesting stuff in there. There are already some release notes, but like the OS itself, they aren’t final yet, and there are still some gaps. Canonical does note that the "oxidization" process – exchanging core Unix tools written in C with new Rust replacements – goes further in this edition: now, the stock OpenPGP encryption support is via the Rust-based Sequoia-PGP. Perhaps one of the most daringly different new features is Canonical’s promised LLM-powered Myna speech-to-text tool. This isn’t installed by default, but you can add it, and a choice of speech-recognition models. We found various sets of instructions, including the unofficial “Ubuntu Handbook”. Our geriatric testbed was a little old for this, though, and we couldn't try it. A couple of weeks ago we took at look at the beta of what will become Fedora 45. Both Ubuntu 26.10 and the default workstation edition of Fedora will use GNOME 51, but since the Fedora beta, the final release of the latest GNOME is here: GNOME 51 “A Coruña”. The version in the Ubuntu beta isn’t working completely smoothly. We saw a persistent error about missing themes, and although the OS offered to install whatever was missing automatically, this failed. Since it doesn’t actually say what is missing, we can’t install it ourselves. The problem is only cosmetic: just some missing icons in applications, very similar to what we saw in Alpine Linux 3.16 four years ago. Sadly, problems around GNOME themes are a long standing issue. As we reported earlier this year, the Linux Mint developers are still struggling with them. The occasional missing icon aside, though, Stonking works pretty well. We tried both in a Virtualbox VM and on bare metal on our old testbed Thinkpad W520, and it ran well in both. The new installation program that arrived with the 2024 LTS version works fine, and now makes it much clearer which control is currently selected with an orange highlight. We do wish the window was resizable, though. The testbed machine has two SATA drives and we had to do a lot of scrolling to choose the right partitions. It also failed to use our dedicated swap partition, although we selected it during installation. Although GNOME 51 removed their support for old Nvidia devices in this development cycle, it still picked up and used the machine’s Nvidia-controlled Displayport output. It didn’t work perfectly: GNOME couldn’t report on the model or properties of our Quadro 1000 GPU, or the CPU-integrated Intel one for that matter, but at least the second screen worked. More surprisingly, it even worked in the Fallback session, even though that uses the Metacity X11 window manager – and while logged into to a Fallback session, it could identify both GPUs. GNOME 51 isn’t a very feature-heavy release, but the Settings app has some useful additions, such as the ability to automatically disable the trackpad when an external mouse is connected. In our testing, it picked up and let us configure mouse, trackpad, and trackpoint, each in a separate tab. GNOME 51 no longer supports Wi-Fi networks with the old WEP encryption system, though. Modern Linux continues to move away from being an OS for old and low-end hardware. If the machine is online during installation, the installer fetches any package updates as it works, so the first update post-install is much quicker. However, this doesn’t apply to Snap packages: the .deb package phase of our first update was very fast, but we got various new snaps. One detail we haven’t noticed before is that while a snap application is updating, its dock icon temporarily gets a progress bar to tell you it’s being updated. We did a full install with all the optional extras, so this applied to Thunderbird as well as Firefox. A full installation took a fairly hefty 13 GB of disk space, although to be fair, that included 4GB of swap space – so in real money, it’s about 9 GB, which isn’t too bad for 2026. According to the htop command, it idles at about 1.2 B RAM, which is quite high, but then GNOME is no lightweight. Linux kernel 7.3 is still in development, but at the time of writing it’s up to RC5, and our testing ran without a hitch. The final version may be out before “Stonking” is completed, but if not, users will get it very soon afterwards. We also gave the Kubuntu desktop a very brief try. In this release, it uses Plasma 6.7.5, and ran well – it was fast, smooth, and happily drove both screens of our testbed machine; helpfully, on our first login, it asked where the second display was relative to the first. If you want modern Wayland niceties such as different dots-per-inch settings on different screens, but you also want a traditional Windows-style layout, KDE is currently the way to go. Plasma 6.8 is scheduled for later this month, and totally drops X11 support. It’s likely to be the desktop in Kubuntu 27.04, making it Wayland-only – so 26.10 is probably the last ever version of Kubuntu in which displaying your desktop thanks to X.org is a supported option. We installed X11 support, which is just one command: sudo apt install -y plasma-session-x11 This brings in multiple extra dependencies, which is why we specified the -y switch, but it took just seconds. We logged out, logged back again choosing “Plasma (X11)”, and… Everything looked absolutely identical. Which is how it should be, of course. Both screens were working normally, thanks to the Nouveau FOSS NVIDIA driver. The only visible differences are the classic “wobbly window” effect when moving windows around, and that the title-bar context menu regains the option to “shade” a window: roll it up, leaving only the title bar visible. You can’t do this in a Wayland environment. Under Wayland, htop reports about 1.2 GB in use; under X.org, about 1.3 GB. The resurrected Oxygen theme from KDE 4 is built in, if you want a bit more visual bling, but we preferred the flatter grayer look of the default Breeze theme. The only freeze that we saw in all our testing of the Stonking beta was after logging out of a Plasma (Wayland) session and trying to log back in using Plasma (X11). To be fair, we suspect most people wouldn’t chop-and-change this much. Ubuntu Stonking is shaping up well. Aside from the small theme-related glitches, GNOME worked fine, and KDE didn’t even have those minor issues. The equivalent beta versions of all the official flavors are also available, including both Ubuntu Unity 26.10 and Ubuntu MATE. Despite a hundred other distros, Ubuntu remains the go-to desktop Linux for most people. While Canonical is getting slightly more experimental with interim releases again, this is a mature product now and they’re a pretty safe bet. ®

7f17f06fe08092b4: TOKYO, Oct 5 — Defending champion Carlos Alcaraz advanced to the final of the Japan Open on Monday after securing a hard-fought 5-7, 6-3, 6-1 victory over fellow Spaniard Jaume Munar in Tokyo.

9c29b4d1a250219c: The first year of Windows 10 Extended Security Updates is coming to an end, and Windows 11's market share has ticked up as enterprises weigh up the cost of keeping Windows 10 running a little longer. Windows 11's market share has risen above 70 percent to 71.5 percent, while Windows 10's has dropped to 27.77 percent, according to statistics wrangler Statcounter. Microsoft does not provide official statistics on Windows 11 and 10 usage, so Statcounter's figures should be treated as estimates. They are derived from Statcounter's tracking code, which is installed on over 1 million sites globally. The shares have remained relatively static since a surge in Windows 11 adoption at the end of last year, likely driven by the upgrade wave after Windows 10 dropped out of support on Oct 14, 2025. The Extended Security Updates (ESU) program allowed holdouts to stick with Windows 10, but the first year of that program is coming to an end, and kind old Microsoft will be hiking the prices for year two, at least as far as commercial customers are concerned. ESU licenses cost $61 per device for the first year for commercial users. Microsoft stated that the price would double every consecutive year for a maximum of three years, meaning that a renewal for year two will come in at $122. There are ways around the charge, of course. As well as consumers who can stay with Windows 10 and receive free security updates in return for redeeming Microsoft Rewards Points or using Windows Backup to sync their settings to the cloud, Windows 365 users are also exempt. It's also worth noting that European Economic Area (EEA) consumers receive no-strings-attached security updates. However, enterprises that need Windows 10 security updates must pay for them, as they did with other Microsoft products the software biz moved on from despite large user bases. The rising cost may be prompting some to reassess their estates. This month's uptick, while far short of last year's surge, could signal a sizeable ripple as the economics of keeping Windows 10 devices supported begin to favor Windows 11. Enterprises have plenty of reasons to keep Windows 10 devices: that one weird bit of hardware that won't work with anything else, or a simple case of a refresh cycle not fitting in with Microsoft's demand that old kit be junked to allow new software to run. Esben Dochy, a principal technology evangelist at Lansweeper, told The Register that its data indicated enterprises had been very active in moving off Windows 10 during the first year of ESU, with what is left being much "stickier." He reckoned there would be a "small bump" around the renewal date, and said, "The ESU price doubles for the second year, and that makes the business case for replacing the 'we'll get to it' machines a lot easier," but noted "it's likely that the steep part of the curve is behind us. "The remaining devices are mostly ones where paying ESU is cheaper or simpler than replacing whatever they're bolted to. For those, ESU really is the cost of doing business." The Statcounter figures indicate that that "small bump" could be on the way as ESU costs double, but many of the Windows 10 hold outs seem unlikely to be going anywhere just yet. ®

17c8e8162aa84d6c: There has been much chilly weather in the sunny meadowlands of AI futures. Fortunately, to use an indecently inappropriate adverb, the rest of the world isn’t really looking, being too busy chewing its nails over the very many other intimations of disaster. Sure, rebel swarms of attack agents breaking out of the labs isn’t a good look. OpenAI delaying its IPO and a new model launch likewise. All these things soak up whatever bandwidth the news media have to AI right now. Putting them in a bigger context, that of promises made and not kept, problems known but not fixed, the observable risk-reward ratios as models develop, we may at last start having a sense of what sort of crisis awaits. Actual crises are frequently triggered by crises in confidence, themselves caused when frameworks of assumption stop standing up to reality and wishful thinking. Thus, the assumption to date is that models will get more powerful and infrastructure more capable, in a way that justifies — demands — massive capex. The economics of giant infrastructure investment when you can’t buy what you need is a great bet in free markets that presupposes that freedom, and yeah, about that. A bigger problem is the idea that more powerful AI is always better. It frequently is, but that’s not good enough, When frontier models have to be kept in LLM jail for uncontrollable dishonesty, not so much. Here, the bigger context is that we’ve known that at heart LLM probability space is entirely relative. There is no ground truth there. Nobody has fixed hallucinations, and now we see the fascinating phenomenon of a machine that doesn’t understand truth but can deliberately lie. If more powerful models are better at that, scratch one assumption. Another huge assumption is that even at the current level of model reliability, agentic architectures are ready to be useful. Those who show all the caution of a chronic gambler on a winning "streak" are as ready to get the brakes slammed on as their opposites. The principal contender for the one true proof of concept that agentic AI is a dangerous fount of unexpected consequence is Meta’s new Muse. It is aimed at low-information credulous users and its star turn is, of course, shopping. The AI use case that’s five years away, and always has been. It’s Meta, so of course it soaks up all the information about you, your online activities and the people you talk to as much as it can. It will soon have ultracute animated Tamagotchi-style pets you can wear around your neck to improve your status as a Meta monitoring post. And we did say it was Meta, so has all the attention to security and careful design you may expect. Which is why it’s already been caught sending people’s physical addresses to strangers, and why when researcher Jonny at neuromatch.social went poking around its infrastructure — each instance runs permanently on its own Linux VM — they found just a ton of fun. Headline party tricks hard-coded. What looks like attempts to train off Claude. And yes, you can get it to run your own things on that VM deep within Meta, which Jonny points out is a botnet paradise waiting to happen. This banger of a bad ‘un is being given away to Meta users, who pretty much define a vulnerable target audience for tech that may not be totally trustworthy. Meta, of course, is dead against AI safety regulation. Place your bets on the headlines to follow. In any case, the upside of using agents as demoed in every keynote is either so trivial and trite — book me a restaurant! — or so catastrophic if it fails — organize my family vacation! — that consumer agents are a bust. It’s just that Meta may be bringing a lot of accelerant to that particular fire. There are other fires, of course, many known about since everything kicked off. Model collapse due to training on data contaminated with output? Still a thing, still no fix a "better" AI might provide. And that habit AI has of retailing everything and paying for nothing, choking off its own training data supply chain and a huge chunk of commerce and culture with it? Very much still a thing. Where AI does make consistent progress is in domain-specific tasks. Science, engineering, mathematics, and coding, if you match a model with enough reinforcement learning with humans who know how to manage them, there are startling results. You don’t get much innovation, not much newness, which is the true driver of progress. Better than humans is highly contextual. Computers have been better at chess for decades, but there isn’t a better chess. Horses run faster than humans, and that’s been useful for four millennia, but we got to peak horses quite some time ago. So the question is, have we reached peak AI, where the cost of future developments don’t match the risk they won’t work well enough to justify? If ChatGPT already writes a perfectly good business letter in a couple of seconds, there is no meaningful improvement to be had for users. Most AI is profoundly annoying, in ways that have nothing to do with the models and everything to do with perverted UX in an attempt to justify growth. That is both unsustainable and a tacit admission that AI hasn’t solved its use case problem. If we are at or near peak AI, is that the crisis that bursts that goddam bubble? Certainly a readjustment, as all bets on the continuous uptick curve are off. AI as it stands is useful enough to power a big industry sector, just in ways that are and remain at odds to how it is marketed and its future fantasies. Trust in AI Max may be shaken, but there's still room for lots of improvement. That slowdown that everyone who isn’t a miscreant is calling for may happen organically, if we escape the smoking-is-good-for-you mentality of the Metans and the Muskovites. That’s still a gamble we shouldn't be taking, but the odds may be better than we thought. ®
568b5b5801f65591: Over the summer I talked to the CEO of Springboards, a startup building an LLM that’s designed to come up with a wider variety of responses than its mainstream rivals do. At the start of the call, he said something that’s been stuck in my head since: “We often say that we’re a self-loathing AI company. We don’t know if we really like what we’re doing.”

“I guess that makes me a self-loathing AI journalist,” I replied. It was a joke! I love my job. But I do not love many of the things the technology I write about has become: warped by hype, steered by zealots, inescapable.
The CEO of Springboards and I are far from alone. Around the world, a love/hate attitude toward AI is very much the vibe right now.

On the one hand, public feelings are souring fast. According to the Pew Research Center, more adults in the US think AI will have a negative impact on them personally, and on society in general, than expect a positive one. The pessimism is strongest among the young.

More than half of people worldwide say that AI products and services make them nervous, according to a report from Stanford University. In a Gallup poll in May, 71% of US adults said they would oppose construction of a new AI data center in their area, far more than the 53% who said they would oppose a new nuclear power plant. And in an NBC poll in March, AI was less popular than ICE.

Yet the number of people using AI is still skyrocketing. ChatGPT hit a billion monthly users in May, according to the market analysis firm Sensor Tower. Google DeepMind’s Gemini is close behind, logging 950 million users in July.

According to Pew, half of US adults now say they use a chatbot, more than twice the number who said they did in 2023. One in four people say they do so every day. And it’s a global habit: More than a third of adults across all 38 OECD countries (a group of the world’s wealthiest democracies) report having used generative AI tools in the last three months.
All these surveys paint a picture of two contradictory truths: A lot of people really do not like AI and a lot of people cannot get enough of it. What’s going on?
It’s possible that these are two distinct groups, but I doubt it. The numbers don’t add up unless the Venn diagram is on its way to being a circle.

It’s also possible that the more people use AI, the more negative their opinions about it will be. There’s at least a correlation to back this up: The Global North, where adoption is highest, skews pessimistic. In the Global South, where adoption levels are lower, people are more optimistic.

But here’s what I really think is going on: When people say they hate AI it’s not the technology they dislike but, rather, the relentless drive of the companies behind it to push the tech upon us in as many ways as possible. They’re telling us to brace for the biggest social and economic upheaval in generations. How do they expect people to feel?

In many ways, we’ve been here before. We saw a similar dynamic play out with social media over the last 20 years. Billions flocked to Facebook and Twitter despite mounting techlash against the companies that ran those services. Ditto for Google search.

With social media there wasn’t much anyone could do. Quitting a platform meant losing all your content and connections, giving you the choice to suck it up or start over. But with AI there’s still a chance for people to have some sway. There’s certainly more political appetite for regulation this time around. All 50 US states have either passed or proposed laws governing the development and deployment of AI, creating a patchwork of more than 2,100 bills across the country—a tenfold increase in three years.

And with a number of top-class open-source alternatives to Google and OpenAI and Anthropic already on the market, there’s also (for now, at least) the potential for more consumer choice and the market pressure that goes with it.

I don’t want to be naïve. Trillion-dollar companies are hard to move. But what comes next is not as inevitable as those companies often imply. When I asked the Springboards CEO why his firm was developing a new model if he didn’t really like AI, he told me there was no walking back from LLMs—but you could still make them do something different.
Here’s hoping we see a lot more of something different: Clarity about what AI can and cannot do and, crucially, a technology that’s not sold as if it’s about to take over the world.

ce35899d8ea8c7e8: There is a question that many non-Malays often ask me, and recently even my wife has raised it: why are Najib Razak and Umno still embraced by Malays, from kampung folk to those with tertiary education?
This question resurfaced following Najib’s conditional pardon allowing for house arrest and Umno’s significant victories in Johor and Negeri Sembilan.
In this article, I present my theory. Readers may find the issue worthy of a research project, or even a PhD thesis!
Reason one: taxation

Many Malays pay little or no tax. For example, my two children, both university graduates, earn about RM4,000 per month and contribute only a few ringgit in taxes. I, on the other hand, pay a substantial amount in tax, but a high-earning non-Malay friend pays four times more than I do.

Because many Malays do not feel the weight of taxation, corruption involving public funds does not resonate with them. To them, money for the people comes from a Malay-led government. As long as salaries, festive aid and allowances arrive, they are content.
Reason two: government employment

A large proportion of Malays work in government. The civil service and political leadership are overwhelmingly Malay – about 80%. Salaries are paid every month, so even if corruption drains RM40 billion, Malay wages remain unaffected.
People may say the country is drowning in debt due to 1MDB, but salaries still come in. Why then should the Malays worry about corruption?
If salaries were withheld for even one month, Umno would collapse and Najib would be cursed. But as long as salaries and allowances flow, corruption has no impact.
Reason three: lack of awareness

Civil servants and Malay businessmen are rarely told that their wages and development allocations – roads, schools, infrastructure – are funded largely by taxes paid by non-Malays employed outside government.

The plundering of billions through corruption does not strike home because Malays do not feel the burden of national debt. Thus, corrupt leaders chosen by Malays borrow from external sources while siphoning off wealth that rightfully belongs to the people.
Reason four: Islamic education
Whether at school or university, this issue is never taught. Even Islamic education avoids it, focusing instead on moral issues like alcohol, gambling and pork.
There are three aspects of Islam that cause corruption to be accepted or ignored:

Religious education itself: I have reviewed thousands of Friday sermons, and none explains how tax money becomes salaries or development funds. Corruption is treated as a minor sin, distant and irrelevant to ordinary people.

Political sermons: Some religious teachers from political parties justify corruption, claiming it is not punishable under hudud because it is absent from classical fiqh texts. So, stealing RM200 shoes may warrant amputation but embezzling RM40 billion is not mentioned. As a result, corruption is seen as less serious than drinking alcohol, not wearing the headscarf, or failing to vote for an Islamic party.

Preachers from abroad: Some insist that Muslims must vote for Muslim candidates, even if they are weak or immoral, as long as they are Muslim. This is compounded by political parties promising heaven for those who vote for them. Thus, corruption, slander and insults will be tolerated if the party claims to uphold Islam in politics.
Reason five: party benefits
Malays receive benefits – haj trips, kitchen aid, bicycles – from Malay parties. No one ever asks where the money comes from.
At restaurants, Malays check for halal certificates, but when receiving party contributions, they never question the source of funds.
Reason six: the DAP bogeyman

8e6652744b8ea4ca: Egyptologists have long debated whether the earliest pharaohs of the First Dynasty were buried with various servants and officials to serve them in the afterlife—a form of human sacrifice. But there is very little archaeological evidence available, given that many of the earliest Egyptian tombs were plundered and/or hastily excavated. A new paper published in the journal Frontiers in Environmental Archaeology reassesses a collection of skulls excavated from tombs in the 1920s and concludes that over one-third show evidence of blunt force trauma. This suggests that they may have been victims of so-called "retainer sacrifice."

Author Roselyn Campbell is a bioarchaeologist at Purdue University who has long been fascinated with the history of human sacrifice. "I'm interested in how we as human beings decide which types of violence are okay and which are not, and how we even define violence," Campbell told Ars. "It's very context-specific. We have to be careful not to extend our own ideas about what violence is and how it's used into other cultures. With Egypt, we have such a long history of European and colonial archeology; they came in with very specific ideas about what this culture was. You really have to make an effort to contextualize the legacy data we have."

Naturally she found the debate over whether ancient Egyptians practiced retainer sacrifice pertinent to her interests. "People tend to fall into one of two camps," said Campbell. "Either retainer sacrifice definitely happened, end of discussion, or it definitely didn't happen, end of discussion. But nobody's actually looked at the bones in a very long time." Forensic science has advanced considerably over the last century, so re-analysis could be useful. Complicating matters is the fact that older sets of remains are often incomplete and/or modified for preservation, destroying vital forensic information in the process.
